title: Contemporary Health Issues
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will delve into the dynamic landscape of emerging and contemporary health issues, gaining insight into their intricate connections with the primary causes of mortality and disability on both national and global scales. By exploring the social, cultural, and environmental determinants of health, you will gain a nuanced understanding of the pivotal factors contributing to health disparities within and between countries. Throughout this unit, you will explore the latest challenges and opportunities in population health, exploring current trends, determinants, opportunities for prevention, and impact on individuals and populations. Moreover, you will have the opportunity to cultivate essential advocacy skills, which will be indispensable for your future career in the health sector.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on contemporary health issues and their interconnections with broader health trends and personal contexts.
Describe emerging and contemporary health issues, including their trends, determinants, opportunities for prevention and impact on individuals and populations.
Outline the social, cultural, and environmental determinants of health and their interplay with the leading causes of death and disability nationally and globally.
Apply an evidence-based approach to advocate for meaningful changes in response to a contemporary health issue, employing a diverse range of communication mediums.

title: I German Studies 6
syllabus_overview: This unit aims to enable students to become independent users of the German language. It provides activities for developing advanced German reading, comprehension, writing and speaking skills and provides students with an opportunity to study German culture extensively. The goal is to develop students' language skills towards C1 level in the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFRL).
learning_outcomes: Identify, evaluate and deploy a broad range of grammatical structures of German at advanced level.
Develop comprehensive advanced level skills in reading, writing, listening and speaking in the German language.
Create meaningful intercultural encounters by applying relevant language conventions.
Identify, describe and evaluate a broad range of aspects of German-speaking cultures and societies.
Demonstrate a refined awareness of language and language use, in both German and in English.

title: Principles in Health and Disease
syllabus_overview: This unit provides the students with the opportunity to explore the relationship between health and disease, from both the biological and psychosocial perspective. The diversity of stressors influencing the human body and mind is explored, and the response of the body to them is discussed. This includes adaptations at both cellular and tissue levels of organisation, inflammation, the immune response, tissue death and neoplasia. The immunisation debate and other relevant public health issues are explored. The relationship between the brain, 'mind', immune and endocrine systems is also studied. By the conclusion of this unit, students will have an understanding of the complex relationship between ourselves and our environment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the appropriate use of terminology, within the disciplines of pathology and microbiology.
Demonstrate a broad knowledge and understanding of medical microbiology and general pathological processes.
Explain the multi-factorial nature of health and disease.
Apply an understanding of the epidemiological aspects of disease, to issues such as immunisation, infection control and disease prevention.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Presentation on the pathogenesis of a condition

title: Health Promotion
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will explore the theories, practices and frameworks of health promotion as a planned approach to the improvement of health in population groups. You will gain an understanding of both local and global health promotion issues, including the determinants of health and how these impact on the planning, implementation and evaluation of health promotion initiatives. You will engage in a mixture of academic texts, case studies, scenarios, and reflective learning practices to immerse yourself in the study of modern health promotion and disease prevention and reduction practices. While designed primarily for health studies students, the unit is also suitable for students from other courses who may be interested the social, economic, political and geographic aspects of this fundamental area of human health endeavours.
learning_outcomes: Describe the various elements that are needed to plan, implement and evaluate a health promotion initiative and be able to apply this knowledge to the development of a health promotion initiative.
Discuss and make informed opinions about some of the social, cultural, economic and political factors that may influence health promotion initiatives nationally and internationally.
Critically analyse some health promotion programs and projects in terms of their application of theories and practices of contemporary health promotion.

Explain the nature of health promotion globally and the effect on health promotion practitioners, with an emphasis on working in teams, across sectors and incorporating continuous flexible learning practices.
Examine and appraise academic writings on the process and application of an evidence-based approach to health promotion initiatives.
Summarise key theories of contemporary health promotion and their connection to health determinants.
Define and describe health promotion and its place within the area of public health, both nationally and internationally.

title: Radiographic Practice
syllabus_overview: This unit develops your knowledge of the key concepts of medical radiation science and radiographic image production, preparing you for future studies in diagnostic radiology. You will be introduced to essential concepts of radiation physics and radiographic image production, processing, and critique. You will learn how to perform and critique radiographic procedures of the musculoskeletal system. You will apply your knowledge of musculoskeletal anatomy and radiographic concepts to assess normal anatomical appearances and explain common variations in radiographic images of the spine and extremities. Additionally, this unit covers the biological effects of radiation, safety concerns, and radiation protection techniques.
learning_outcomes: Identify and assess normal radiographic anatomy of the musculoskeletal system and explain variations in appearance due to radiographic technique (Scientist and Scholar)
Explain the working principles of diagnostic imaging modalities and critically appraise how they influence image production (Scientist and Scholar)
Discuss legal and ethical considerations related to radiography and radiation use and strategies to ensure public safety (Professional)
Summarise the properties and biological effects of x-rays and explain how they interact with matter, influence image quality, and inform patient safety standards (Scientist and Scholar)
Discuss and demonstrate competency in obtaining radiographic images of the musculoskeletal system as applicable to chiropractic practice (Clinical Practitioner)

title: Pathology and Diagnosis I
syllabus_overview: This unit builds on the knowledge base of pathophysiology acquired in Principles of Health and Disease (HLTH2301). It examines the aetiology, epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation and differential diagnosis of common conditions of the cardiovascular, haematopoietic and lymphatic, endocrine, digestive and respiratory systems. Case studies are used to develop the ability to create a differential diagnosis based on clinical presentation and examination. The complexity of disease is discussed within the biopsychosocial framework that will deepen student understanding of the complex relationship between ourselves and our environment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the fundamental skills required for decision-making and clinical reasoning on the basis of aetiology, pathophysiology, epidemiology and clinical manifestations
For each disease studied, explain the relationship between its aetiology, pathophysiology and clinical manifestations
Explain the multifactorial nature in the development of disease states

Describe the aetiology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, pathophysiology and clinical manifestations for a range of pathologies that occur in each of the following systems: Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Haematopoietic and Lymphatic, Endocrine and Digestive systems
Apply knowledge of anatomy, physiology, biochemistry and basic pathology, to develop the likely mode of progression of the diseases studied in this unit

assessment_tasks.task_name: End of semester final written examination

title: Pathology and Diagnosis II
syllabus_overview: This unit continues to build on the knowledge base of pathophysiology and examines the aetiology, epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation and differential diagnosis of common conditions of the nervous, musculoskeletal, renal, reproductive and integumentary systems. Case studies are used to develop the ability to create a differential diagnosis based on clinical presentation and examination. The complexity of disease is discussed within the biopsychosocial framework that will deepen student understanding of the complex relationship between ourselves and our environment.
learning_outcomes: Integrate your knowledge of the aetiology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, pathophysiology, and clinical presentation of common disorders
Identify the common pathologies that can occur in the nervous, musculoskeletal, renal, reproductive and integumentary systems.
Explain the multifactorial nature of the development of disease states.
Compare and contrast diseases on the basis of aetiology, pathogenesis, pathophysiology and clinical manifestations
Demonstrate fundamental skills required for decision-making and clinical reasoning necessary for differential diagnosis

title: Master of Research - Health Sciences
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: The 8000-level components of the Master of Research are not designed around units. The thesis and its revision together with core research activities form a single coherent research unit which consists of the following: Research Proposal: through your reading of the literature in your field and in consultation with your supervision team, you will develop a plan for your research project.This will be delivered as both a written and oral presentation. You will attend school and/or faculty-run seminars and engage in activities that develop your knowledge of the sub-disciplinary field in which you want to situate your own research. Literature Review: You will produce a draft of your own literature review for your thesis. Thesis: you will complete a research project and write it up in a short thesis of approximately 20,000 words. Oral Presentation: you will deliver a talk on your research findings. You will revise your thesis to address comments provided by examiners.
learning_outcomes: be effective and coherent communicators to both specialist and non-specialist audiences, and demonstrate high-level discipline-specific research and technical skills
demonstrate a deep knowledge of, and apply expert judgement on, contemporary local and/or global disciplinary issues
apply critical and integrative thinking to problems, concepts and theories within their disciplinary field through scholarly investigation of currently available evidence
be responsible ethical and reflective researchers able to work independently and lead and collaborate within teams to enhance disciplinary knowledge to the benefit of individuals and communities
be socially and culturally responsive researchers, who collaborate effectively with industry, community and their broader disciplinary field
be future focused and adaptable, demonstrating critical thinking and analytical skills to synthesise and advance the knowledge base of their discipline

apply advanced knowledge and skills to plan, undertake and complete distinct research projects using appropriate research methods aligned to complex and novel research questions within their field or discipline

demonstrate an independent ability to apply their knowledge and skills as ethically responsible and reflective autonomous researchers committed to lifelong learning and discovery to advance their disciplinary field

demonstrate problem solving skills and creativity through their ability to apply existing knowledge and produce new knowledge in innovative ways to enhance their field or discipline and deliver significant benefits to the broader community
demonstrate an understanding of complex research systems to effectively develop impactful solutions to global problems

title: Research Methodologies in Health
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will develop practical skills to design a Public Health research project. You will develop knowledge and skills on how to conduct literature reviews, select appropriate research methods including when to use quantitative and qualitative methods and synergies between them, how to collect data, understand research governance and ethics application process, and develop a research proposal. You will apply these skills in the context of a research topic in an area of your interest.
learning_outcomes: Develop a clear understanding of the application of qualitative research principles. (Scientist & Scholar)
Demonstrate research communication skills required for the dissemination of research information. (Practitioner)
Apply a systematic approach to purposefully reviewing public health literature to inform research. (Practitioner)
Formulate explicit research questions/objectives relevant to public health enquiry. (Scientist & Scholar)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Oral examination of qualitative research principles

title: Infectious Disease Epidemiology
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will gain an understanding of how infectious diseases, from tuberculosis to COVID-19, have significantly impacted on human populations. You will focus on infectious disease epidemiology to learn about how diseases spread both locally and globally. You will explore the concepts of source of infection and immunity, surveillance as a tool for understanding burden of disease and impact of control strategies, and outbreak investigations to identify sources and management of disease spread. You will explore these themes through case studies such as sexually transmissible diseases, HIV/AIDS and vaccine preventable diseases. You will also explore current out-break investigations and infectious disease surveillance methods; and will learn how key aspects of, and innovations in, infectious disease management have impacted on public health law, management and policy.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate how control of infectious diseases has impacted on public health law and policy. (Citizen)
Describe the principles of infectious disease epidemiology. (Scientist & Scholar)
Critically review and evaluate surveillance systems for infectious diseases. (Practitioner)
Apply the principles of outbreak investigation in the context of containing infectious diseases. (Practitioner)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case studies in infectious disease monitoring and control

title: Global Nutrition and Food Security
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: Optimal nutrition is a cornerstone to health and well-being. In this unit you will develop an understanding of the relationships between nutrition, food security and health in Australia and globally. You will learn about key nutrients for human health in terms of their function, dietary sources and different nutritional requirements at various life stages; and then explore the factors that influence dietary behaviours and habits and their relationship to chronic diseases. You will learn how to evaluate methods used to determine nutritional status and explore nutrition related policies, guidelines and programs used to prevent unhealthy dietary behaviours and consequently reduce the prevalence of chronic conditions. Finally, you will explore global nutrition issues related to nutrition transition, food security and environmental sustainability.
learning_outcomes: Integrate knowledge of nutrition and food security issues with the design of effective and culturally appropriate strategies or interventions to address these issues. (Practitioner)
Apply appropriate dietary assessment measures for individuals and populations. (Practitioner)
Discuss the environmental impact and sustainability of current dietary patterns. (Citizen)
Identify the key nutrients essential for human health, their role, requirements and dietary sources and analyse the factors impacting dietary intake and behaviour. (Scientist & Scholar)
Identify major diet-related health issues and critically analyse interventions aiming to address them. (Scientist & Scholar)

title: Program Planning and Evaluation in Health Promotion
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will learn to plan and evaluate health promotion programs and assess their implementation and impact. You will apply knowledge and learnings from the classroom to real world scenarios using a pragmatic lens. This unit will prepare you to work as a health promotion practitioner, in settings such as local health districts, non-government organisations, and community enterprises.You will work as individuals and in groups, similar to working on a real project. To be successful in this unit you will need to have a solid understanding of disease prevention and health promotion.
learning_outcomes: Identify and articulate appropriate research designs and methods for designing and evaluating a health promotion program. (Practitioner)
Critically appraise the strengths and limitations of a health promotion program. (Scientist & Scholar)
Apply the principles of planning and evaluation to real world scenarios with a pragmatic approach. (Citizen)
Describe the key principles of planning and evaluation of health promotion programs. (Professional)

title: Public Health Project Management
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will review the key stages of a health-related project, from conception to completion. Topics covered will include project design and planning, identifying key project contributors and stakeholders, launching the project, managing ongoing activities, troubleshooting and handling changes, maintaining records, effective communication and networking, disseminating findings, and finalising the project. By completing this unit, you will gain a comprehensive understanding of how to successfully deliver a health-related project from start to finish.
learning_outcomes: Apply understanding of project management techniques in health. (Practitioner)
Evaluate best project troubleshooting approaches and the required associated steps. (Practitioner)
Evaluate how to design and deliver a project plan including ethical and integrity considerations. (Scientist & Scholar)
Demonstrate skills in communication and self-directed learning. (Professional)
Describe the coordination of a health-related project with a diverse multidisciplinary team. (Citizen)
Critically evaluate components and deliverables of a project. (Practitioner)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Retrospective review of a health related project.

title: Academic Communications in Public Health
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: This unit is designed to support you in your Master of Public Health course by equipping you with knowledge and skills you need to effectively communicate using academic and discipline-specific language, texts and conventions. You will not only develop your oral and written communication skills but also your critical reading and reflective thinking skills to gain in-depth insight into diverse perspectives and your own learning processes to become more active and informed problem solver and communicator. Both independent and collaborative approaches to learning are employed to develop strategies for independent learning as well as teamwork.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical thinking and information literacy skills in the assessment and interpretation of information from various sources. (Practitioner)
Produce written and multimodal texts appropriate to the purpose and audience in accordance with academic, disciplinary and professional communication conventions. (Practitioner)
Apply principles of acceptable academic practices, behaviours and values (academic integrity) in the completion of assessment tasks and other learning activities. (Professional)
Demonstrate purpose- and context-driven communication skills in public health. (Practitioner)

title: Foundations of Public Health
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: This unit will provide you with the foundations for understanding the field of public health and build your knowledge and skills towards becoming a public health practitioner. You will be introduced to the core functions of public health with attention to the role that different health fields and disciplines play in contributing to health protection and promotion in diverse communities and populations. You will gain an understanding of different public health models, approaches and perspectives, and learn to apply these to analysing contemporary public health issues. This foundational unit will equip you with practical skills essential in moving forward your studies and future public health practice.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse priority public health issues relevant to specific populations or communities with consideration of diverse influences, such as social, environmental, and policy factors. (Citizen)
Analyse the role of different health professions and disciplines in developing effective population health solutions. (Professional)
Demonstrate effective communications skills in the context of professional public health activities. (Practitioner)
Explain public health and its core functions in maintaining, improving, and protecting the health of communities and populations. (Scientist & Scholar)

title: Determinants of Health
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: This unit examines fundamentals of determinants of health in two modules. In the first module, you will learn about social, behavioural and structural determinants of health. In the second module, you will be introduced to biological and environmental factors that impact health status of individuals and populations. You will explore the linkages between determinants of health, and how this impact individuals and communities. This will encapsulate concepts related to what supports good human health, and what contributes to human illness. You will explore contemporary and emerging challenges to public health and develop conceptual and practical knowledge essential for a career in public health.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the significance of cultural competency and the development of collaborative partnerships with diverse communities in advancing public health . (Citizen)

Analyse and evaluate the needs of vulnerable populations by examining the impact of race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and age demographics on these communities and populations. (Scientist & Scholar)
Apply different methodological and preventive approaches to the determinants of health. (Practitioner)

Analyse and evaluate the complex interplay of social and environmental factors at individual, community and societal levels and their impact on the health of individuals and populations. (Scientist & Scholar)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Viva/oral poster presentation on determinants mapping

title: Introduction to Epidemiology and Biostatistics
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces you to the skills of scientific inquiry and appraising evidence which are fundamental to public health research and practice. You will engage in integrated learning about reporting data, study design, data analysis and interpretation, and critical appraisal of research papers in public health. By completing this unit, you will gain knowledge and skills which will enable you to locate, produce and appraise evidence in the field of public health.
learning_outcomes: Calculate and interpret the epidemiologic measures of occurrence and association in order to assess public health impact. (Scientist & Scholar)
Identify and explain data commonly used to report on health at a population level. (Scientist & Scholar)
Critically appraise public health research papers using an epidemiological framework. (Practitioner)
Characterise study designs used in public health and evaluate their strengths and limitations. (Practitioner)

title: Disease Prevention and Health Promotion
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: Health promotion creates supportive conditions for health, enabling people to have control over, and improve their health and wellbeing. Health promotion officers need to have a good understanding of health promotion approaches and behaviour change models in order to engage communities and enable people to address their health needs. In this unit, you will develop an understanding of health promotion concepts, frameworks and theories used to formulate policy and develop programs tailored for a variety of settings. The unit is taught with an emphasis on the determinants of health and health inequities, including economic, social and environmental influences. The key skills you will develop include designing and evaluating evidence-based health promotion initiatives within a specific population/community. These skills will prepare you for a career in health promotion practice and research.
learning_outcomes: Design and evaluate health promotion strategies to demonstrate effective application of values and principles, ethics and theoretical models of health promotion. (Practitioner)
Analyse the range of factors that influence the health of individuals and populations, including social determinants of health and lifestyle behaviours. (Citizen)

Critically analyse and apply the range of theoretical and practical intervention frameworks available for disease prevention and health promotion delivery within a specific population/community. (Scientist & Scholar)
Explain and apply key health promotion concepts and principles in planning and practice. (Scientist & Scholar)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Health promotion program - design and evaluation

title: Systems Science in Healthcare
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: Health care systems are complex consisting of many interacting components, people and perspectives. You will learn about systems theories (for example, resilience, consumer participation, and sociotechnical perspectives) and apply them to examine policy and practice underpinning public health problems. The unit is delivered by experts in health systems, including digital health informatics, safe systems and systems evaluation methods. You will learn through guest lecturers, interactive activities and assessments requiring you to analyse and evaluate real-world case studies and health interventions.
learning_outcomes: Examine the current discipline of systems thinking and how it underpins healthcare. (Citizen)
Discuss the rationale for adopting a systems approach to address population health issues. (Scientist & Scholar)
Examine the role of digital health and health informatics in systems thinking. (Scientist & Scholar)

Analyse and apply a range of theoretical concepts related to systems thinking including resilience, sociotechnical systems, safe systems, consumer participation and systems evaluation methods to public health issues. (Practitioner)
Examine the challenges of adopting a systems approach to public health. (Citizen)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Mapping interactions between health system components

title: Leadership, Teamwork and Advocacy
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: This unit focuses on leadership, teamwork and advocacy with the development of key practical skills in these areas for a career in public health. You will explore leadership theory while reflecting on your own experiences, helping you grow into a future public health leader. You will also learn to apply reflective thinking to your public health practice and implement innovative ideas to address complex public health issues. You will develop skills to collaborate and communicate effectively in multi-disciplinary teams of diverse backgrounds and in different contexts. You will work in groups to plan and deliver your own advocacy campaign to address contemporary public health issues. Real world examples are used throughout this unit and there is an emphasis on practical learning experiences.
learning_outcomes: Apply reflective thinking in relation to your own leadership capability by drawing on practical experiences and leadership knowledge in a culturally safe, respectful and inclusive manner. (Citizen)
Apply theoretical knowledge to real-world scenarios by collaborating to create an advocacy strategy and campaign that addresses a contemporary public health issue. (Practitioner)
Examine leadership theory and frameworks in the context of public health. (Scientist and Scholar)
Demonstrate an understanding of the mechanisms through which public health advocacy advances population health. (Scientist and Scholar)

title: Public Health Capstone
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: This unit will provide you with an opportunity to draw together and reflect on your learning across the course and align this to the core public health competencies. You will collaboratively investigate a specific public health challenge, applying your knowledge to analyse the issue and develop innovative solutions. Your efforts will culminate in a presentation that showcases your findings and recommendations. You will present your work to peers, faculty, and industry partners, enhancing your communication and collaboration skills essential for your future career in public health.
learning_outcomes: Apply public health knowledge and skills to an authentic and collaborative public health task. (Practitioner)
Develop a project deliverable and communicate the findings to a public health audience. (Practitioner)
Demonstrate leadership and advocacy skills by collaborating with community and/or industry partners to address a public health. (Citizen)
Reflect on your learning and development as a public health practitioner using an academic framework aligned with core competencies. (Professional)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group presentation on public health challenge

title: Public Health Professional Practice
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: This unit provides you with an opportunity to gain experience in the Public Health workplace. By undertaking this placement unit, you will have the opportunity to contribute to real-world initiatives in areas as diverse as policy, research, health promotion, and advocacy. Tasks may involve ethics submissions, program development and evaluation, literature reviews, and stakeholder engagement. You will have the opportunity to discuss and plan your placement with MQ staff and workplace supervisors. Placement will consist of approximately 11 weeks of part-time placement. Entry to this unit is subject to a quota and satisfactory interview performance. Students intending to enroll in the unit should consult with the Unit Convenor.
learning_outcomes: Apply public health knowledge and skills in the partner organisation. (Practitioner)
Reflect on the ability to effectively work within a public health organisation. (Professional)
Communicate effectively with public health professionals. (Citizen)
Demonstrate the understanding of the requirements for developing a workplan related to public health professional practice. (Scholar & Scientist)

title: History of Indigenous Education
syllabus_overview: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations have been sharing knowledge for over 65,000 years. This unit explores many of these older ways of teaching and learning and inter-generational knowledge transmission. This unit also examines how Western education practices and policies have impacted Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people since colonisation. Racism and the exclusion of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people from various public-school systems is investigated.
learning_outcomes: Develop a strong theoretical basis to understand the injustices Indigenous Australians face as a legacy of colonialism.
Demonstrate a critical awareness of historical education policy and strategies targeted specifically towards Indigenous Australians.
Examine how various forms of racism have impacted the education outcomes of Indigenous Australians.
Confidently use online communication forums and engage in informed interactive learning.
Understand the longevity of Indigenous practices of teaching and learning.

title: Sociology of Education
syllabus_overview: This unit offers students a range of skills that will equip them as effective educators across a range of social and cultural divides. The unit is interested in what constitutes 'good pedagogy' in a general sense, and how effective teaching and learning can be applied specifically to Indigenous teaching and learning contexts. The unit will provide students with the critical skills necessary to question and evaluate a range of considerations pertaining to critical pedagogy, and it will encourage prospective teachers to re-think some of their pre-conceived ideas about the relationship between teachers and learners. It will also equip future teachers of Indigenous students with a skill-set appropriate to cultural competencies and pedagogical expectations.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrated high level of written communication skills including structuring and supporting an academic argument.
Demonstrated high level of competency in the ability to research independently, think critically and evaluate and apply course content.
Understand how to apply effective teaching and learning practices to Indigenous students/cohorts.
Think critically about the roles of teachers and learners.
Understand the theoretical origins and practical application of critical pedagogy and Indigenous critical pedagogy.
Confidently use online communication forums and engage in informed interactive learning.

title: Indigenous Languages and Teaching
syllabus_overview: This unit examines the ongoing impact of colonisation and colonial systems on the revitalisation and teaching of Indigenous languages. Students will develop an understanding of the efforts made by Indigenous peoles to revitalise, maintain and teach their languages. The unit will explore the importance of local languages and cultural knowledges within a teaching and learning context. Students will engage in Community Consultation and the development of a teaching resource that incorporates Indigenous language.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrated understanding of the diversity of Indigenous languages in Australia.
Demonstrated ability to develop teaching resources that incorporate Indigenous languages.
Demonstrated knowledge of protocols, and ethical practices including meaningful consultation associated with the use and teaching of Indigenous languages.
Understand the importance of embedding local Indigenous languages and cultural knowledges within teaching programs.
Confidently use online communication forums and engage in informed interactive learning.
Demonstrated high level of written communication skills including structuring and supporting an academic argument.
Understand the ongoing impact of colonisation on Indigenous languages loss and the activism by Indigenous peoples to revitalize and maintain languages.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Indigenous languages learning and teaching plan

title: Rethinking Indigenous Education
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces students to radical thinking and alternative models of education. Students will engage with Indigenous and Black scholarship that envisions the abolition and replacement of existing models and practices of settler colonial education. Students are encouraged to imagine radical global futures that are shaped by Indigenous peoples, communities and knowledges. Graduates of this unit will be proficient in abolitionist, futurist and Indigenist thinking.
learning_outcomes: Critically engage with exisiting education systems
Evaluate your own position as an educator
Demonstrate proficiency in abolitionist, futurist and Indigenist thinking
Demonstrate high level of written communication skills including structuring and supporting an academic argument.
Demonstrate comprehension of Indigenous and Black scholarship on transformative education

title: Global Indigenous Education
syllabus_overview: While exploring education from the perspectives of Indigenous people in Australia and in other parts of the world you will gain a better understanding how education has been used as a tool for the colonial project. This unit focuses on education and Indigenous people from Australia, Aotearoa (NZ), Canada and the United States. These particular countries cover hundreds of distinctive Indigenous communities who exist across contemporary national boundaries and geo-political divisions. Although these communities are linguistically and culturally diverse, they nevertheless share common colonial histories of dispossession and ongoing political, economic and social marginalisation and subjugation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrated high level of written communication skills including structuring and supporting an academic argument.
Understand the concept of ‘global solidarity’ and the continuity of Indigenous activism.
Understand the ways in which Indigenous peoples continue to teach Indigenous knowledges.
Understand the impact of colonisation on the diverse cultures and knowledges of Indigenous peoples globally.
Confidently use online communication forums and engage in informed interactive learning.
Critically examine the Declaration of Human Rights and demonstrate an understanding of its impact on Indigenous peoples throughout the world.
Demonstrate a strong theoretical basis of the historical injustices Indigenous peoples throughout the world have faced and the impact this has had on their education.

title: Indigenous Research Theory and Practice
syllabus_overview: In preparation for conducting research, this unit provides an opportunity to develop a hypothetical research project that supports students to develop their skills prior to engaging in research involving human subjects. The unit covers topics from conceptualising a research project, developing a research proposal including design and methodology, applying for ethics approval and ensuring research is best practice, ethical and promotes meaningful engagement and reciprocity between researchers and Indigenous people and communities.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, identify and evaluate issues concerning research in Indigenous contexts.
Demonstrate a high level understanding of the ethical and methodological requirements of research with Indigenous people and communities.
Confidently use online communication forums and engage in informed interactive learning.
Demonstrated high level of written communication skills including structuring and supporting an academic argument.
Demonstrate knowledge of Indigenous methodologies and the ability to apply them to research.
Critically reflect on your responsibilities as a researcher.

title: Politics, Power and Indigenous Education
syllabus_overview: This unit examines the relationship between politics, power and colonialism and education as it relates to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander populations. By examining a range of government policies and legislation students will gain a more detailed understanding of the social, cultural, economic and political impact on Indigenous people. This unit also focuses on contemporary and historical Indigenous led activism in relation to education.
learning_outcomes: Examine the implications that colonialism has had on Indigenous Australians’ rights and access to education.
Demonstrated high level of written communication skills including structuring and supporting an academic argument.
Explain how government policy and legislation has and continues to impact Indigenous Australians socially, economically, and politically.
Critically analyse the political positions of historical and contemporary texts.
Demonstrate effective use of theories of power to analyse the impact of politics on Indigenous Australians.

title: Trauma Informed Education
syllabus_overview: Trauma and intergeneration trauma continue to impact Indigenous communities in Australia and around the world. This unit will provide a detailed understanding of trauma and trauma informed education as it relates to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, children and communities. It is a multi-disciplinary unit that aims to increase skills including being able to apply critical thinking, collaborative practices and judgement when working individually and within communities across service provision with children, families and communities experiencing ongoing trauma.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrated knowledge of trauma and intergenerational trauma that impacts Indigenous people and communities.

title: Grand Challenges and Systems Thinking
syllabus_overview: This foundational unit in the Bachelor of International Studies immerses students in the real-world challenges that societies and industries will face in the coming decade. Through an interdisciplinary lens, it introduces ‘grand challenges’ - complex global problems marked by ambiguity and interconnectedness that can't be addressed through siloed thinking. Students begin developing core skills in systems thinking, exploring how cultural, political, historical, and ethical factors intersect to shape global issues. Students examine recurring patterns and drivers of change and learn to understand complex systems, while engaging with live challenges facing industry, government, and community partners. Interactive and scenario-based activities provide hands-on experience in scoping problems, breaking them into components, and understanding their wider context. This experiential, exploratory environment fosters creativity, critical thinking, and multidisciplinary collaboration. By the end of the unit, students will have started developing foundational capabilities in analysing complex systems, and a human-centred, adaptive mindset for tackling global challenges.
learning_outcomes: Apply foundational systems thinking concepts to complex global challenges.
Map the interconnected social, cultural, historical, and ethical factors shaping contemporary global problems using system mapping techniques.
Collaborate on scenario-based activities that address ambiguous and multifaceted global issues.
Identify patterns and dynamics to understand drivers of societal change.

title: Understanding Global Systems: Power and Governance
syllabus_overview: Who holds power in the world, and how is it exercised? This unit introduces students to how power operates in the global system through governance, contestation, and the structures of the world economy. It focuses on three core frames (state power, global governance, and political economy) that provide a foundation for interpreting international affairs. Students will examine theories and concepts of international politics, and key actors and structures including states, international organisations, trade and security frameworks, corporations, and transnational movements. Case studies and scenario-based activities illustrate how systems emerge, evolve, and interact across local, regional, and global contexts. The unit explores how agendas are formed and challenged, how global power is distributed and disrupted, and how economic structures shape political outcomes. Institutions such as the United Nations, regional organisations, and global trade frameworks are studied alongside contemporary dynamics including rivalries between established (and emerging) global powers, the role of middle powers, and multilateral cooperation in a fragmented order. By the end of the unit, students will have a structured framework for understanding the systems that underpin global affairs and will be prepared to apply this knowledge in subsequent units of the Bachelor of International Studies.
learning_outcomes: Apply analytical tools to identify the interconnections between actors, interests, and norms in real-world complex systems.
Investigate the relevant implications of global decisions and governance structures from diverse stakeholder perspectives.
Identify the structures, actors, and institutions underpinning global governance and political systems.
Develop an understanding of the distribution and contestation of power across societies, institutions, and international systems.

title: Ways of Knowing: Interdisciplinary Thinking for Global Challenges
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces students to the power and limits of different disciplinary approaches to global challenges. Complex problems rarely fit within a single field, so students in this unit explore how the humanities, social sciences, STEMM, and business frame global issues, and how integrating these perspectives can unlock new possibilities for analysis and action. Through contemporary case studies, students will examine how cultural interpretations, economic models, scientific methods, and technological innovations approach the same problem, and how they can converge to offer robust and innovative analysis. Students develop skills in recognising disciplinary assumptions, bringing methods into dialogue, and reflecting on how knowledge systems shape definitions of and solutions to global problems. By the end of the unit, students will have a critical foundation for developing innovative, cross-sector strategies and human-centred responses to global change.
learning_outcomes: Design interdisciplinary ways to approach human-centered solutions for unpredictable global change.
Identify and describe approaches to creating knowledge across disciplines and perspectives.
Compare disciplinary approaches from the humanities, social sciences, STEMM, and business to address complex global challenges.
Explore the role of emerging technologies, including AI, in enabling interdisciplinary responses to problems.

title: Unlearning Culture: Myths, People, and Change
syllabus_overview: This unit invites students to question and “unlearn” taken-for-granted assumptions about culture. Too often, culture is used as a simple explanation for complex human behaviour, social tensions, or political outcomes, and obscures deeper realities. In this unit, culture is approached as a dynamic, evolving process shaped by power, identity, language, and history. Students explore how cultural meanings are created and contested across diverse contexts, with a focus on Australia and the Asia-Pacific as sites of global cultural exchange. Case studies highlight how migration, transnational connections, and historical narratives shape cultural identities today. Students also examine how identity is communicated, meaning negotiated, and dominant myths challenged. Through applied activities, students will practice cultural intelligence and strategic storytelling, using diverse formats to communicate cultural complexity across diverse audiences. By the end of the unit, students will be equipped to foster dialogue and engage constructively with unfamiliar cultural challenges in a rapidly changing world.
learning_outcomes: Explore approaches to cultural intelligence in relation to people, identities, and narratives.
Analyse how power, identity, language, and history shape cultural meanings in diverse global contexts.
Create multimodal artefacts to communicate cultural complexity using digital storytelling.
Identify relevant frameworks to investigate processes of cultural change.
incompatibilities: INTS1000: Language and Communication: Cultural Contexts

title: Cultural Influence and Power
syllabus_overview: Who decides what counts as “normal,” “right,” or “true”? This unit explores how knowledge and influence are constructed and circulated across cultural, historical, and institutional settings. Students examine the role of language, norms, and identity in shaping how societies understand truth, authority, and legitimacy. Drawing on interdisciplinary approaches, the unit introduces key concepts on the cultural and communicative dimensions of power. Case studies from different regions and sectors illustrate how governments, media, and communities use symbols, stories, and strategies to shape public perception, and how individuals and groups resist or reframe dominant narratives. Students reflect on their own role within systems of influence and begin to build the cultural intelligence needed to collaborate across difference. By analysing how power is acquired, maintained, and contested, the unit provides a foundation for understanding leadership, communication, and change-making in a complex world.
learning_outcomes: Communicate insights about cultural power relations using digital storytelling for professional audiences.
Analyse how cultural narratives, artefacts, and symbols shape power dynamics in local and global contexts.
Apply systems thinking to map the interplay between cultural identity and authority in real-world scenarios.
Evaluate the impact of historical and contemporary power structures on leadership and influence in cross-cultural settings.

title: International Studies Beginners In-Country Cultural Studies
syllabus_overview: This unit is offered on a pass/fail basis and designed for students who wish to complement their academic program through a short-term residential program relevant to their study of Languages and Cultures. This unit facilitates study at a partner university where intensive learning will take place in the student’s target language and in regards to a topic relevant to their discipline. The program of study at the overseas institution will be approved and promoted in collaboration with Macquarie International. The short period of intensive study is intended for students already studying a language at Macquarie, ideally those who are taking or have completed the introductory level(s). Participants will be selected for the program based on their application, suitability, and the relevance of the program to their degree.
learning_outcomes: participate in diverse communities and collaborate with others on tasks.
identify that language and culture interact, and relate that interaction to real-word situations and problems.

show awareness of differences and similarities between language use in their native language or culture and the target language or culture, as well as thoughtful understandings of how to negotiate difficulties that arise during cross-cultural and/or cross-linguistic interactions
increase their ability to clearly express, detail, defend, and/or promote ideas in public situations, through their native language and/or target language

title: Intercultural Language Project 1
syllabus_overview: Can various experiences, practices and perspectives of a culture tell us something unique about that culture? This project-based unit seeks to promote a greater awareness of, and engagement with, lived experiences in the broad context of the intersection of language, culture and society. It focuses on helping students broaden their appreciation of aspects of intercultural life and practices as well as sites of meaning in a culturally and linguistically specific environment. Through a semi-guided project, students will be encouraged to explore one aspect of intercultural life by reviewing, collecting and analysing relevant data related to a specific language and cultural context.
learning_outcomes: Design and conduct a project-based activity in an intercultural context within and outside the university environment.
Demonstrate adequate library and information retrieval skills relevant to the nominated project.
Collate, analyse and evaluate data collected during intercultural encounters.
Demonstrate capacity for self-organisation and effective project management.
Communicate a targeted aspect of language specific cultural life to peers, teachers and the public using written, oral and/or digital media in a detailed and comprehensive manner.
Identify ways in which society and culture interact and locally manifest in a specific cultural context.

title: Global Citizenship and Leadership
syllabus_overview: What does it mean to be a global citizen in a time of disruption, inequality, and rapid change? What kind of leader could you become? This unit explores global leadership not as a title, but as a dynamic relationship between self, society, and system. Students consider how citizenship, belonging, and responsibility shape leadership across local and global contexts, from health and education to business, advocacy, sustainability, and diplomacy. Drawing on humanities and social sciences perspectives, the unit examines how leadership is shaped by culture, politics, and history. Students analyse diverse models of leadership (including feminist, Indigenous, distributed, and transformational approaches) and explore how communities mobilise to drive change. Students will also investigate leadership failures, developing the capacity to navigate disagreement, create shared purpose, and act ethically. Students identify their own strengths, commitments, and values, reflecting on how their experience connects with leadership domains that matter to them. By the end of the unit, students will have begun to shape their leadership identity and understand how values and experiences can contribute to collaborative, human-centred change.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical reflection to assess your own leadership style and global citizenship competencies.
Collaborate to address a global workplace challenge, demonstrating teamwork and intercultural skills.
Develop inclusive leadership strategies for engaging diverse teams and stakeholders globally.
Examine the principles and ethical responsibilities of global citizenship in professional contexts.

title: Technology and Society: From Plato to NATO
syllabus_overview: What happens when technology doesn’t just support human life, but reshapes what it means to be human? This unit introduces foundational debates in the human-technology relationship, exploring how communities have imagined, adopted, resisted, and transformed technologies across time. Technologies are never just neutral tools: they reflect cultural values, shape social norms, and operate within systems of power and politics. Through case studies ranging from ancient philosophy to Cold War infrastructures and contemporary artificial intelligence, students examine how technologies influence, and are influenced by, the societies that produce and regulate them. Key themes include technological determinism versus social shaping, innovation and inequality, the influence of technology on human interaction and communication, and the long history of imagined futures. Drawing on insights from culture, politics, history, philosophy, linguistics, anthropology, and media, the unit develops a critical vocabulary for interrogating technology. By the end of the unit, students will be able to interrogate current debates on technology, assessing what a technology does, who it serves, how it evolves, and why it matters.
learning_outcomes: Construct systems maps to visualise the interconnections between technology, society, and power in selected case studies.
Trace the evolution of technological thought and practice identifying key philosophical, historical, and cultural shifts.
Differentiate the societal impacts of major technological innovations across historical periods and cultural settings.
Articulate complex ideas about technology’s role in society using multimodal communication.

title: Navigating Digital Worlds
syllabus_overview: How do platforms, algorithms, and data systems shape how we live, work, and relate to one another? This unit explores the digital infrastructures embedded in everyday life, from social media feeds and predictive text to biometric scans and algorithmic recommendations. Rather than focusing on technical skills, students analyse these systems as cultural and political forces that influence identity, behaviour, and opportunity. Topics include platform design, data ethics, surveillance, digital labour, and bias in AI. Students will investigate how algorithmic decisions affect everything from job applications to dating, and how digital environments reinforce or challenge norms around gender, race, class, and power. A core feature of the unit is working with generative technologies through prompt development and reflection. Students will learn how prompts shape both ideas and outputs, and how interacting with AI involves a form of co-authorship between human intention and machine logic. Prompt-writing becomes a method for interrogating what these systems value, who they centre, and how they construct meaning. By the end of the unit, students will be equipped to critically map the digital systems shaping their world, and ask informed, ethical questions about their design, impact, and future.
learning_outcomes: Investigate how digital platforms and technologies mediate identity, community, and participation in contemporary societies.
Demonstrate digital literacy by curating, navigating, and ethically participating in online environments.
Assess the risks and opportunities of digital engagement for individuals and groups across cultural and social contexts.
Produce multimodal content that communicates insights about digital life to varied audiences and professional settings.

title: Strategic Communication and Cultural Narratives
syllabus_overview: How do we understand ourselves through the stories we tell about ourselves? How do we understand others through the stories we do and don’t tell about them? This unit offers students a rich grounding in concepts and tools that will allow them to communicate thoughtfully, strategically, and effectively across cultural, institutional, and digital boundaries. By critically examining representation, misinformation, cultural exchange, and the impact of technology on narrative form, students engage with the ethics of storytelling and identity construction. They learn how meaning is shaped and contested, and how communication strategies adapt and evolve to across cultural norms and shifting platforms. The unit investigates how media and storytelling influence public, corporate, and civic discourse, and how communication can be used to negotiate values and mediate conflict. Emerging technologies like generative AI are introduced as cultural artefacts embedded in systems of power and bias and innovation. Students experiment with digital platforms and AI tools, reflecting on ethical use and implications for messaging. Through workshops and digital artefact creation, the unit will enable students to build competencies in cross-cultural messaging, stakeholder engagement, and adaptive storytelling, preparing them to navigate the world with cultural intelligence and persuasive impact.
learning_outcomes: Apply futures thinking methodologies to anticipate emerging global narratives and their potential impacts.
Evaluate the impacts of current cultural discourse and social narratives on local, intercultural, and global policy and planning.
Design adaptive strategies that address uncertainty and complexity in global systems caused by media and frontier technology.
Develop scenario-based models that explore alternative futures using interdisciplinary and diverse stakeholder perspectives.

title: Cultural Intelligence and Problem Solving
syllabus_overview: In this unit, students apply and extend interdisciplinary tools, mindsets, and methods introduced in the first year of the Bachelor of International Studies. They engage with complex, real-world challenges, scoping, framing, and proposing interventions in response to simulated global issues or live projects with external partners. Building on previous units, students use systems thinking, cultural intelligence, and cross-sectoral analysis to navigate uncertain problem spaces. Through iterative activities, they map stakeholders, identify leverage points, analyse constraints, and frame actionable responses in contexts such as public health, global institutions, and business. The unit centres on a structured, open-ended challenge from contemporary social, environmental, political, or technological domains. Students collaborate to develop strategic proposals linked to cutting-edge research or the Faculty's Humanities Lab partnerships. While solutions may remain open-ended, the focus is on learning to work productively within complexity, scoping challenges, understanding systems, and testing interventions. Students leave with stronger skills in interdisciplinary projects and teamwork, systems-based framing, and adaptive planning which is vital for their final-year studio, immersions, and careers in volatile contexts.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on personal lens, pre-conceptions, and expertise and how these influence interactions, decision making and problem solving.
Analyse cultural intelligence frameworks to respond to intercultural challenges.
Create models and scenarios addressing global challenges by integrating diverse stakeholder perspectives.
Communicate design solutions using multimodal and narrative techniques to diverse audiences.

title: International Studies Intermediate In-Country Cultural Studies
syllabus_overview: This unit is offered on a pass/fail basis and designed for students who wish to complement their academic program through a short-term intensive program relevant to languages offered in Languages and Cultures. This unit facilitates study through a partner university where intensive learning will take place in the student’s through the partner institution will be approved and promoted by Languages and Cultures Discipline in collaboration with Macquarie International. The short period of intensive study is intended for students already engaged with issues of language and culture in their course studies. Participants will be selected for the program based on their application, suitability, and the relevance of the program to their degree.
learning_outcomes: Increase their ability to clearly express, detail, defend, and/or promote ideas in public situations, both through their native language and their target language.
Skillfully interact and/or work with others to accomplish tasks, build communities, and collaborate with people from diverse backgrounds

Show awareness of differences and similarities between language use in their native language and the target language, as well as thoughtful understandings of how to negotiate difficulties that arise during cross-cultural and/or cross-linguistic interactions.
Express nuanced understandings of how language and culture interact, and evidence ability to apply the target language to solving real-word tasks.

title: Intercultural Language Project 2
syllabus_overview: Can various experiences, practices and perspectives of a culture tell us something unique about that culture? This project-based unit seeks to promote a deeper understanding of, and engagement with, lived experiences in the broad context of the intersection of language, culture and society. It focuses on helping students expand their appreciation of aspects of intercultural life and practices as well as sites of meaning in a culturally and linguistically specific environment. Through a semi-guided project, students will be encouraged to explore one aspect of intercultural life in the Australian context by collecting and analysing community-relevant factual data.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate extensive library and information retrieval skills relevant to the nominated project.
Communicate a targeted aspect of language specific cultural life to peers, teachers and the public using written, oral and/or digital media in a nuanced and sophisticated manner.
Design and conduct a project-based activity in an intercultural context within and outside the university environment.
Identify ways in which society and culture interact and locally manifest in the Australian context.
Collate, analyse and evaluate data collected during intercultural encounters.
Demonstrate proficiency in self-organisation and effective project management.

title: Narrative and Authority
syllabus_overview: How do leaders use stories to build trust, mobilise support, or claim legitimacy? And how are those stories challenged, contested, or rewritten? This unit explores leadership as a narrative practice - a process of shaping meaning, asserting values, and negotiating power across diverse audiences. You will examine how stories function not only as reflections of leadership, but as tools that establish authority, frame crises, and mediate between conflicting worldviews. You will analyse how leadership narratives are constructed, rejected, appropriated, or silenced, and how these dynamics shape whose voices are heard and whose are excluded. Drawing on global case studies and media examples, you will investigate how leadership narratives operate in political leadership, corporate communication, diplomacy, and activism. Engaging with theories of narrative framing, legitimacy, and discourse, you will consider how leaders navigate persuasion and representation in an era of misinformation, identity politics, and algorithmic influence. Through practical exercises in storytelling and media analysis, you will experiment with crafting strategic narratives. By the end of this unit, you will be equipped to frame issues clearly, recognise storytelling as both a leadership tool and a contested site of power, and use narrative as a core site of persuasion and change.
learning_outcomes: Create persuasive narratives addressing contemporary leadership challenges in international settings.
Analyse how narrative strategies are used to construct and challenge authority in global leadership contexts.
Apply critical frameworks to assess the legitimacy of competing authorities in global affairs.
Evaluate the effectiveness of storytelling in influencing public opinion and organisational change.

title: The Ethics of Decision-Making: Power in Global Systems
syllabus_overview: What does it mean to make a ‘good’ decision amidst uncertainty? This unit explores how ethical reasoning and leadership intersect in real-world settings shaped by power, responsibility, and uncertainty. Students will examine decision-making, from global health and humanitarian response to corporate responsibility and climate action. Analysis of contemporary and historical case studies will illustrate how political and cultural forces shape decisions, how leaders navigate competing obligations and constraints, and how ethical theories influence norms in complex contexts. Students will explore how power operates not only through visible authority, but also through norms, institutional logics, and systems of belief that shape which decisions seem possible, acceptable, or inevitable. Cross-cultural comparisons will challenge students’ assumptions and deepen their understanding of ethical leadership. Using simulations, collaboration, and futures-thinking tools, students will develop skills to strategically navigate ethical dilemmas with clarity and cultural intelligence. By the end of the unit, they will understand what constitutes a legitimate or persuasive decision, and how trust, transparency, and accountability are built or lost through leadership practice. These are the essential foundations for leadership in volatile, fast-changing environments.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate how power and agency shape ethical outcomes in international organisations.
Communicate the implications of ethical decisions to diverse stakeholders in professional settings.
Analyse ethical dilemmas in global decision-making using relevant theoretical frameworks.
Apply ethical reasoning to propose solutions for complex, real-world global leadership challenges.

title: Ethics and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: How do we respond when innovation outpaces regulation, and when technologies meant to help begin to harm? This unit introduces the ethical challenges posed by emerging technologies, from AI and automation to digital surveillance, climate tech, and biotech. Students explore how technologies often produce unintended consequences: not because they are flawed in design, but because they interact with social systems in complex and unequal ways. Through sector-based case studies, including health, finance, education, and public safety, students will investigate how data bias, opaque algorithms, environmental cost, and system inequity shape real-world outcomes. They will learn to work with ethical frameworks that go beyond simple yes/no judgments, and engage in futures thinking to anticipate long-term risks, competing values, and stakeholder priorities. This unit emphasises critical judgment under uncertainty. It allows students to practise identifying ethical dilemmas, analyse trade-offs, and reflect on their values as a future leader or practitioner. By the end of the unit, they will be able to evaluate emerging technologies not only in terms of innovation, but in terms of responsibility, inclusion, and the kind of social futures they help create or prevent.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the consequences of emerging technologies for justice, equity, and the public good.
Present ethical arguments and recommendations effectively to both specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Interrogate competing ethical frameworks and their relevance to contemporary social and technological challenges.
Formulate ethical solutions to complex, real-world dilemmas involving technology and society.

title: Human Futures: Norms, Disruption, and Transformation
syllabus_overview: How do societies decide what is “normal”? What happens when ideas, actions, or technologies disrupt the norms that shape systems, behaviours, and futures? And how can those norms be strategically disrupted to enable transformation? This practice-based unit explores disruption not as chaos, but as a method for leading change in social, political, and technological systems. In a lab-style environment, students analyse how norms are established, internalised, and defended, and experiment with how change can be effected from both inside and outside institutions. Students work through simulated scenarios that ask what change is for, when a system needs to break, who decides, and how to intervene ethically. Using tools such as futures wheels, narrative prototyping, stakeholder mapping, and design sprints, students identify leverage points, test interventions, and explore how transformation can happen from within institutions or at their edges. Through guided practice, students learn to recognise hidden norms, reframe assumptions, and contribute to futures that are not only possible, but desirable. This unit prepares students for higher-level applied work with partners and communities in their final year.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate strategies for navigating cultural transformation in global settings.
Analyse the impact of emerging technologies and disruptions on global and local norms.
Design adaptive solutions to address unpredictable change in human centred systems.
Apply foresight methods to anticipate and plan for future leadership challenges.

title: Designing with Technology: Industry Studio
syllabus_overview: How do we design technologies that work not just technically, but ethically, equitably, and in context? In this applied studio, students tackle real-world challenges with industry, community, or civic partners to prototype or critically evaluate emerging technologies. The focus is on translating ethical insights and human-centred values into practical design decisions, considering not just what technology can do, but what it should do in specific social settings. Working in teams, students engage in structured design processes such as stakeholder mapping, field research, and prototyping. They explore how cultural norms, power dynamics, and lived experiences shape how technologies are adopted, adapted, or resisted, and how to design for usability, accessibility, and cultural relevance. This unit is not about coding or engineering, but about working across disciplines to bring critical insight and design awareness to complex social problems. Final projects may include speculative prototypes, scenario plans, engagement strategies, or design recommendations co-developed with external briefs. By the end of the unit, students will be ready to contribute to real-world tech conversations, as collaborators, strategists, and ethically engaged designers.
learning_outcomes: Engage with industry, community, and/or civic problems within multidisciplinary teams.
Demonstrate feasible solutions or provocative experiments through effective team and stakeholder collaboration by defending and discussing project viability, impact, and scalability.
Create context-appropriate solutions or new ways of understanding real-world problems using emerging technologies through iterative design.
Apply humanities-based critical analysis to evaluate and communicate about the ethical, cultural, and power implications of emerging technologies.
Build your own skills in using emerging technologies through risky play and critical reflection.

title: International Studies Intercultural Program
syllabus_overview: This unit is a core requirement of the Bachelor of International Studies (BIS) and is offered on a pass/fail basis. Completion of this unit is generally through an immersive program taken primarily in the language and culture of the student's BIS specialisation. Students who do not meet the entry criteria for exchange-based INTS3000 programs may be eligible for a modified program. Alternatives to undertaking an exchange program are available where undertaking exchange is not possible (for documented, unavoidable, and serious reasons). To be eligible to enrol in INTS3000, students will need to complete INTS3000 application milestones and demonstrate clear degree progression criteria related to WAM and intermediate or above language outcomes. More information on these milestones and criteria will be communicated to BIS students via student email in their first session of enrolment. Students must ensure they are aware of the requirements and must ensure that they begin the application process for INTS3000 at least one year in advance.
