title: PACE: Global Futures Challenge Lab
syllabus_overview: In this capstone unit, students bring together the full mindset and skillset of the Bachelor of International Studies to tackle a real-world, interdisciplinary challenge. Through a live project with community and industry partners, students apply systems thinking, cultural intelligence, and stakeholder engagement to model and respond to long-term global trends in uncertain environments. Working in diverse teams, they engage in a studio-based process of strategic problem-solving, supported by workshops in project design, narrative framing, and cross-sector communication. Students experiment with digital tools and generative AI, critically assessing their potential and limitations. The focus is not just on what students create, but how they work iteratively, ethically and collaboratively, across boundaries of discipline, culture, and practice. This unit marks the culmination of the degree, where students synthesise their academic and applied learning in a final, forward-facing project. Graduates leave the unit with a portfolio-ready outcome, equipped with the skills, knowledge and confidence to lead adaptive, collaborative responses to global challenges.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the effectiveness and sustainability of proposed solutions using appropriate metrics and feedback.
Showcase the application of your refined interdisciplinary toolkit through professional presentations to diverse audiences.
Implement collaborative projects with industry or community partners addressing real-world challenges.
Design innovative solutions to complex global challenges by applying interdisciplinary knowledge to strategic foresight.

title: Intercultural Immersion
syllabus_overview: This unit offers students the chance to apply their learning in real-world cultural contexts; locally, internationally, or through virtual collaborations. Guided immersion deepens cultural intelligence, ethical awareness, and adaptability across unfamiliar social and institutional settings. Whether via overseas study tours, local community projects, or partner-engaged collaborations, students engage in structured, relational learning grounded in ethical reflexivity. Preparatory workshops provide research methods, ethical frameworks, and cultural protocols, while debriefing sessions support reflection on experiences and their academic, personal, and professional relevance. Students will apply their interdisciplinary toolkit to analyse norms, complexity, practices, and power systems. They will critically reflect on their positionality, communication style, and relational dynamics of their cross-cultural experiences. By the end of the unit, students will have developed advanced skills in cultural analysis, cross-boundary collaboration, and ethical engagement, all of which are essential for global careers in diplomacy, NGOs, policy, and international-facing industries.
learning_outcomes: Design a framework for collaboration that accounts for cultural and geopolitical complexities relevant to your immersive experience.
Enact skills and knowledge of cultural, political, and social practices to work adaptively across unfamiliar environments.
Apply cultural intelligence frameworks to navigate intercultural contexts through immersive engagement.
Reframe responsive approaches to global challenges by integrating diverse knowledge systems and stakeholder perspectives.

title: International Studies Project
syllabus_overview: This unit uses key themes to explore language and cultural contexts. Students will work in groups with relevant staff in Languages and Cultures undertaking projects in one of the languages and cultures offered in the Department. Assessment is by individual projects which allow students to accomplish identified goals in relation to literature, theatre, film, music, fine arts, education, or linguistics, to examine relationships between language and culture and demonstrate the application of advanced skills in languages and cultures. Students will use language(s) they are studying to deepen their understanding of and communicate specialist knowledge in language or culture. Students need to have at least upper intermediate language skills and have completed prior units of study in languages and cultures and articulate their intended project goals in their enrolment request.

communicate deep knowledge of a specialist topic in language and culture.
apply independent and analytical judgment to a research, professional or language accreditation project.
organise and manage a project plan to accomplish an identified goal.
critically evaluate resources, prioritise relevance and apply to achieving an identified goal.

title: Language, Literature, Translation: Intercultural Perspectives
syllabus_overview: Reading across cultures and languages enables intercultural understanding. This Unit offers students intercultural perspectives on the study of literature and translation across different languages. It introduces students to the history and theory of literatures beyond national, linguistic and cultural borders. Students will learn to interpret these literatures by applying relevant literary theories to them. They will interrogate the concept of cultural translation by considering what is at stake in the translation of texts across languages and related cultures. In practical terms, students will then consider the choices made when translating literary texts by reading case studies and through their own creative translation practice. Lectures will be delivered in English. Tutorials will facilitate students applying speaking, listening, reading and writing skills in the target language and culture.

title: Uncertainty, Strategy, and Foresight
syllabus_overview: What does it mean to lead when the future is uncertain, the data incomplete, and the risks complex? In this unit, students will develop the skills and strategic mindset to navigate volatility, not by predicting the future, but by preparing to shape it. This unit looks at patterns, ruptures, and how past decisions shape present constraints and future possibilities. Uncertainty is explored as a condition of leadership rather than a failure of planning. Exploration of global case studies and speculative scenarios, students will examine how organisations, sectors, and communities respond to emerging challenges, from political instability and technological transformation. They will practice identifying the key components of global challenges and their local impacts in order to model plausible futures, lead through ambiguity, and communicate vision under pressure. Through horizon scanning, backcasting, and scenario planning, students will blend creativity and systems thinking with applied strategy to anticipate long-range consequences, test alternative pathways, and imagine adaptive responses to complex problems. By the end of the unit, students will be equipped to examine how futures are framed (as utopian, dystopian, crisis-driven, or inevitable), whose futures are imagined, whose are excluded, and how different communities interpret uncertainty.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the effectiveness of risk management approaches in complex international environments.
Design scenario-based plans for responding to unpredictable global events in professional contexts.
Apply strategic foresight tools to develop leadership strategies for navigating uncertainty in global settings.
Communicate strategic recommendations to diverse audiences using professional formats.

title: Decisions Gone Wrong
syllabus_overview: Why do smart decisions fail? Why do leaders with data, expertise, and intentions still face backlash, breakdowns, or unintended consequences? This unit explores what happens when leadership decisions go wrong, not as a failure of logic, but of alignment, interpretation, and context. Across government, business, global institutions, and multilateral systems, students will analyse cases where decisions fell apart because leaders ignored the cultural, political, or interpersonal conditions that make success possible. They will learn to analyse breakdowns in communication, motivation, trust, and cross-cultural understanding. Through simulations and scenario analysis, students will experiment with how to recover from missteps, navigate conflict, and re-establish legitimacy. Along the way, they will develop practical tools for stakeholder analysis, diplomatic negotiation amidst uncertainty and tension, and collaborative learning under pressure. By the end of the unit, students will be equipped to lead with greater self-awareness, cultural intelligence, and strategic capacity in uncertain conditions.
learning_outcomes: Analyse historical and contemporary cases of failed leadership or decision-making in global organisations.
Communicate critical reflections on failure and recovery to professional and public audiences.
Evaluate the causes and consequences of poor decisions using interdisciplinary leadership frameworks.
Apply lessons learned from failure to propose improved decision-making strategies for future leaders.

title: Human Technology-Interface: Beyond the Frontier
syllabus_overview: Technology evolves in its technical sophistication, and in how it reshapes societies, institutions, and human lives. What can the past teach us about today’s technological futures? This unit explores how major technological shifts (from the printing press to platform capitalism, from industrial automation to biotech) reshape how societies organise themselves, how institutions evolve, and how humans imagine what comes next. Technologies are not just inventions; they are systems that evolve through culture, politics, and ideology. You’ll trace historical and cultural pathways of key technologies and use them to question present assumptions about innovation, disruption, and inevitability. What counts as “progress”? Who drives it, who resists it, and who benefits? Drawing on humanistic approaches across studies of culture and societies you’ll critically assess the narratives that accompany new technologies (from AI to bioengineering) and consider what futures they imply. Rather than forecasting what’s coming, you’ll learn to identify patterns, ruptures, and recurrences - the cultural rhythms that help us contextualise present-day tech debates and anticipate future turning points. By the end, you’ll be equipped to examine emerging technologies not just as objects of use, but as evolutionary systems shaped by human values, contested meanings, and structural power.
learning_outcomes: Forecast the cultural and geopolitical implications of emerging technologies by conducting strategic, evidence-based trend analysis.
Distinguish recurring patterns in the adoption, adaptation, and contestation of frontier technologies across different societies and eras.
Examine how human-technology interfaces have evolved in response to cultural, social, and geopolitical shifts across historic and contemporary contexts.
Synthesise and communicate insights about human-technology interaction and its future trajectories to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Designing Change: Leadership Lab
syllabus_overview: In this final-year studio, students apply the full Global Leadership and Communication toolkit to a real-world problem. They will respond to a live challenge brief drawn from sectors such as government, civil society, international organisations, or community partnerships. Working in professional teams, students analyse stakeholder dynamics, explore leverage points, and design interventions such as campaigns, strategic narratives, prototypes, or policy proposals. This unit focuses on leadership in practice: building alignment, navigating ambiguity, and translating insight into influence. It engages with the live problems that industries face in order to create deliverables designed to influence real-world systems and stakeholders. Students will work iteratively: testing ideas, receiving feedback, and adapting strategies under changing conditions. They will critically reflect on their own leadership style and capacity to examine how they lead across differences, negotiate complexity, and stay grounded in values while aiming for impact. By the end of the unit, students will produce a tangible outcome for a professional portfolio, and the confidence to lead collaborative, strategic change in uncertain and dynamic contexts.
learning_outcomes: Design and implement a change initiative addressing a real-world global leadership challenge.
Apply leadership and project management skills in a collaborative, practice-based context.
Communicate project outcomes and leadership insights to a professional audience.
Critically evaluate the impact and sustainability of change initiatives using appropriate professional metrics.

title: I Italian Studies 6
syllabus_overview: In this unit students develop their ability to follow complex lines of argument in spoken and written texts in Italian in a range of genres and to identify and extract key information. The unit focuses on practicing skills in expressing and defending sophisticated arguments and opinions and employing strategies to understand and respond to unfamiliar material in preparation for applying language knowledge to social and professional situations. Students will use their judgement in decision-making around communicative tasks (written, oral, spontaneous and prepared) in meaningful everyday contexts.
learning_outcomes: Identify, evaluate and deploy a broad range of grammatical structures of Italian at advanced level.
Identify, describe and evaluate a broad range of aspects of Italian-speaking cultures and societies.
Develop comprehensive advanced level skills in reading, writing, listening and speaking in the Italian language.
Create meaningful intercultural encounters by applying relevant language conventions.
Demonstrate a sophisticated awareness of language and language use, in both Italian and in English.

title: Technology Gone Wrong
syllabus_overview: Why do some technologies thrive in one context and fail in another - not because they don’t work, but because they don’t fit? This unit explores what happens when technologies “go wrong” in cultural, political, or institutional contexts that were not anticipated by their designers. You’ll examine case studies where success in one setting became failure in another - from consumer products and entertainment platforms to infrastructural technologies and digital governance tools. These failures aren’t just glitches or poor design: they reveal deeper misalignments between technology and the values, expectations, or power dynamics of the societies they enter. You’ll analyse examples such as global media misfires, platform censorship, interface localisation failures, or technological resistance in health, gaming, and urban systems. Drawing on insights from tech law, media studies, cultural politics, and global governance, you’ll develop tools to diagnose why technologies succeed, falter, or are rejected in different places. By the end of the unit, you’ll understand how context - not just code - determines what technologies mean and how they function. You’ll be able to map sociotechnical systems, evaluate political and cultural fit, and anticipate the ethical and strategic risks of deploying tech across boundaries.
learning_outcomes: Diagnose systemic risks and unintended outcomes associated with technological innovation and deployment.
Devise strategies for preventing or mitigating failure in future technology projects.
Investigate historical and contemporary cases of technological failure and their social, ethical, and political consequences.
Disseminate lessons learned from technology failures to professional and public audiences.

title: Human-Tech Intervention: Technology Lab
syllabus_overview: What does it take to lead in a tech-saturated world? In this capstone-style unit, you’ll apply the full toolkit of the Humans and Emerging Technologies major to a real-world challenge. Working in teams, you’ll collaborate with external partners — from civic organisations to industry or research networks — to design an intervention that addresses a pressing technological issue with social, ethical, or cultural dimensions. You’ll use tools such as systems mapping, futures thinking, and values-based design to frame the problem, engage stakeholders, and propose a tech-enabled response. This might take the form of a speculative prototype, public engagement strategy, policy intervention, or cross-sector design recommendation. This unit is not about building the next app - it’s about leading change at the human-technology interface. You’ll critically reflect on your own leadership capacity, navigate complexity in live project work, and work iteratively across disciplinary boundaries. By the end of the unit, you’ll have a portfolio-ready outcome and the experience of collaborating with others to shape technological futures — not just as users or critics, but as ethical, strategic, and culturally attuned practitioners of change.
learning_outcomes: Co-create a technology-driven intervention using human-centred and ethical approaches with industry or community partners.
Showcase project outcomes to diverse audiences using digital and professional platforms.
Operationalise the intervention, adapting to feedback and real-world constraints in a dynamic environment.
Critically evaluate the impact and sustainability of the intervention using data and reflective practice.

title: I Italian Studies 5
syllabus_overview: In this unit students proceed to a deeper understanding of the structure of the Italian language and develop skills in all areas of the Italian language (reading, writing, listening and speaking) to an advanced level of proficiency. Students learn to discuss a wider range of topics as well as substantially increase their knowledge of vocabulary. Emphasis is placed on contemporary standard Italian in the widest possible context and students will develop an awareness of regional variations of the language and the use of dialects. Much attention is given to the active use of the language. This unit also focuses on further increasing students' skills in intercultural communication so that they will be able to communicate in a manner which is culturally as well as linguistically appropriate. Interactive seminar activities based on the use of authentic Italian language materials, provide students with opportunities to use Italian as much as possible.
learning_outcomes: Identify, evaluate and deploy the grammatical structures of Italian at advanced level.
Identify, describe and evaluate nuanced aspects of Italian-speaking cultures and societies.

title: I Japanese Studies 1
syllabus_overview: This unit provides introductory Japanese language instruction for students with no previous knowledge of Japanese. Students develop basic speaking, listening, reading & writing skills, including mastery of the hiragana & katakana scripts. By the end of the course, students should be able to describe their surroundings, ask questions, make plans, and effectively participate in a variety of fundamental conversations. Furthermore, the unit will also assist students in developing an awareness of sociocultural issues which influence Japanese language use. The unit provides opportunities for interactive language learning, and a wide variety of methods for Japanese practice through the use of online resources.

syllabus_overview: This unit will improve students' understanding of Japanese grammar, vocabulary, culture, and writing so that they can accomplish a variety of practical and authentic tasks. Students will develop their listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills to a level where they can carry out a wide variety of common social interactions, and participate effectively in multiple communicative contexts. Additionally, students will gain basic proficiency in the use of the kanji script, and the ways that standard written Japanese employs kanji, hiragana, and katakana in tandem. The unit provides opportunities for interactive language learning, and a wide variety of methods for Japanese practice through the use of online resources.

Identify, evaluate and deploy the grammatical structures of Japanese at elementary level.

title: Exploring Japanese Literature
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces students to Japanese literary works and is designed to enhance their understanding of Japanese literature in linguistic, socio-cultural and historical contexts. The unit will cover the ancient to the current period through diverse texts such as poetry and all forms of narratives including i-novels, fantasies and thrillers. It will also examine rich intertextuality found in Japanese literature, as exemplified in manga/anime works inspired by the Japanese classical masterpiece, The Tale of Genji .

title: Japanese Media and Culture
syllabus_overview: This unit provides a comprehensive overview of Japanese contemporary culture through critical reflection and analysis of Japanese media. Placing a particular focus on the study of popular culture as a site to acquire sophisticated understandings of Japanese society, students will gain advanced insight into the socio-cultural, political, and economic influences which shape contemporary Japan. Working with authentic Japanese media texts, the unit builds students’ Japanese cultural literacy and prepares them for careers in either Japan or which require significant engagement with Japan. Further, the unit situates the study of Japanese contemporary culture within the broader context of the global media landscape, extending students’ intercultural communicative competence through engagement with a range of sources in both Japanese and English. Students will complete reflective and persuasive writing tasks based in critically engaging with Japanese media, developing advanced skills in research and communication.

Situate and explicate understandings of Japanese contemporary culture through critical reflections on Japan’s positioning in the global media landscape.

title: Social Issues in Contemporary Japan
syllabus_overview: This unit explores various issues in contemporary Japanese society, investigating how Japanese people navigate these issues and develop strategies of support and resistance to structural inequalities. Through engaging with authentic Japanese media texts and scholarship, students to develop critical analytical skills to identify and articulate the role of culture in the production of social issues in Japan. The unit is divided into four "modules": 1) Precarious Japan, 2) Gender and Sexuality, 3) Ethnic Minorities, and 4) Japan in the World. Topics covered include: cultural dynamics of the contemporary family; politics and civil society; economic cycles of boom and stress; environmental issues and tipping points; the pathway to adulthood; reconstructions of gender, Japanese sexual minority cultures; ethnic difference and communities; minorities and social peripheries; and Japan's place in the broader world.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a high level of intercultural communicative competence through class participation and engagement with authentic Japanese media texts.
Generate reasoned, considered and original analysis and evaluation of authentic Japanese media texts, both orally and in writing.
Demonstrate detailed knowledge of a wide range of aspects of Japanese culture and society by drawing upon authentic Japanese media texts and scholarship.

title: Foundations of Law
syllabus_overview: This unit will enable students to attain the key legal skills (legal research, reasoning, and writing; applying precedent; statutory interpretation; and legal problem solving) and to acquire the foundational legal knowledge (Australia legal institutions; legal theory; comparative legal systems; parliamentary process; role of the judiciary) necessary for further study in law.
learning_outcomes: Work independently, meet deadlines and take initiative.
Apply principles of statutory interpretation and the doctrine of precedent to interpret primary legal sources (case law and legislation) for the purpose of deriving legal rules and principles.

Locate relevant primary and secondary sources through legal research using online databases, library resources and internet sources.

title: Japanese Studies in Action
syllabus_overview: This unit aims to serve as a transition to the next stage of a student’s career, whether that is entry into the workforce or pursuing further study, by providing an opportunity to reflect on and consolidate the knowledge and insights developed through your degree into a significant project. Students will be expected to demonstrate their knowledge in Japanese Studies (language and/or content/area studies) through the project. To successfully complete this unit, it is essential that you exercise your own initiative in managing your project/tasks and work collaboratively and engage with your group members.
learning_outcomes: Independently produce clear, reasoned, well-structured oral and/or audiovisual and/or written material, which are correctly referenced.
Make effective use of time and resources for efficient and timely planning and completion of tasks.

title: Contracts
syllabus_overview: The law of contracts is a fundamental area of study for an undergraduate degree in law and serves as the basis for a variety of later core and elective units. This unit equips students with a knowledge of essential doctrinal principles of contract law and the capacity to apply legal problem solving skills to the resolution of contractual disputes. It covers the formation of contracts, the contents and interpretation of contractual terms, the vitiating factors affecting contract formation, the discharge of contractual liabilities and other related issues such as formal requirements, illegality and privity of contract. In addition, the unit conveys an understanding of the main competing philosophies of contract and the practical role of contracts in a broader social and historical context.

Explain the role of contracts in an historical and social context.
Formulate, present and evaluate oral and written arguments about contract law, drawing upon relevant precedent and policy considerations.

title: Law, Lawyers and Society
syllabus_overview: In this unit students are introduced to applied legal ethics and the law that governs the roles and responsibilities of solicitors and barristers in Australia. The unit covers the history and profile of the legal profession, the development of ethical reasoning and application of ethical systems to legal practice. Students will study the legal and philosophical problems confronting lawyers, including confidentiality, access to justice, truth in the adversarial system, conflicts of interest and relationships between lawyers, clients and the community. They will learn how the legal profession is regulated and analyse the effectiveness of the professional disciplinary regime. The unit also introduces students to general skills of ethical problem solving and to the importance of sound communication skills for the practice of law.
learning_outcomes: Communicate, interact and collaborate professionally and effectively in verbal and non-verbal contexts across diverse settings.

title: Criminal Justice
syllabus_overview: This unit aims to develop in students a critical understanding of substantive criminal law - what makes an accused guilty or not guilty of a crime. Students will learn the principles of criminal responsibility and the defences available to an accused, and then apply that knowledge to a range of crimes including murder, assault and property offences. Students are encouraged to consider if the criminal law of NSW is rational, fair and just, and how it has been shaped by historical, social, political and philosophical factors.
learning_outcomes: Apply principles of statutory interpretation and problem solving methods to criminal justice scenarios
Identify how the criminal law of NSW has been shaped by historical, social, political and philosophical factors
Explain general doctrines of criminal responsibility and outline elements of offences and defences in accordance with Priestley requirements for legal practice
Work independently, meet deadlines and take initiative.
