Assess and utilise clinical case scenarios and the latest scientific research to describe, critically analyse and communicate basic concepts of diseases learned in this unit.
Identify systemic and local responses of the body to tissue injury and infection.
Describe common biological and genetic mechanisms of neoplastic transformation and development.
Evaluate the dynamic relationship between microorganisms and humans, and methods of microbial identification and control.
incompatibilities: HLTH2301: Principles in Health and Disease
MEDI2005: Human Health and Disease Processes

title: Digital Health Systems for Community, Child and Family, and Aged-Care Services
syllabus_overview: This unit focuses on the design, implementation, and management of digital health systems tailored for community health, child and family services, and aged care. You will explore how these technologies enhance service delivery and improve health outcomes while engaging with ethical considerations and sustainability practices. By completing this unit, you will gain the knowledge and skills necessary to contribute meaningfully to the field of digital health, driving improvements in service delivery for community, child and family, and aged-care services.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the digital health needs of community, child and family, and aged-care services. (Scientist and Scholar)

Demonstrate effective communication skills in conveying key concepts of digital health systems to diverse stakeholders, including healthcare professionals and patients, in a socially and culturally respectful manner. (Citizen)
Discuss the ethical implications, data privacy, and security considerations, as well as sustainability practices relevant to digital health technologies in your chosen service area. (Professional)
Design a conceptual model for a digital health system and implement a prototype to assess its effectiveness. (Practitioner)

title: Musculoskeletal System
syllabus_overview: This unit delves into the musculoskeletal anatomy and physiology of the upper and lower limbs, as well as the trunk. Through practical classes featuring prosected cadavers, anatomical models, medical imaging, surface anatomy, and clinical case studies, you will apply your theoretical knowledge in a hands-on environment. By adopting an integrated, clinically-based teaching approach that includes relevant gross and radiological anatomy, histology, and embryology, you will gain a comprehensive understanding of the human musculoskeletal system.
learning_outcomes: Identify surface anatomy landmarks of the limbs and back, and the course and distribution of major nerves and blood vessels.
Explain the structural and functional characteristics of the musculoskeletal components in the limbs and back.
Outline the development and basic histological features of the musculoskeletal system.
Explain the role of the endocrine system in the regulation of muscle and bone homeostasis.
Apply knowledge of the musculoskeletal system to the analysis of clinical cases and medical images.
Articulate the physiological basis of bone and muscle function, and mechanisms of tissue repair after injury.
incompatibilities: ANAT1002: Anatomy of Limbs and Back

title: Alimentary System
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will develop an in depth understanding of the anatomy, physiology and biochemistry of the alimentary system. You will be provided with a unique learning experience that encompasses anatomy wet laboratory sessions, simulation laboratory classes, and interactive tutorials. Gross and surface anatomy will be taught alongside gastrointestinal physiology and the major metabolic pathways (carbohydrate, protein and fatty acid metabolism). You will engage in clinical problem solving supported by relevant medical and scientific literature and discuss the ways in which scientific advances translate into clinical practice.
learning_outcomes: Describe the anatomy of the gastrointestinal system, including structural components and structural organisation of the abdominopelvic wall and viscera.

Discuss case studies by organising and integrating knowledge of gastrointestinal structures and functions (as well as concepts of pathophysiology) and by critically evaluating evidence from scientific and medical literature.
Describe the hormonal mechanisms that regulate food intake and metabolism.
Explain anatomical and physiological changes that occur in common gastrointestinal diseases.
Describe the pathways involved in the metabolism of glucose, fatty acids and amino acids.
Describe the physiology of the gastrointestinal system, including regulation of motility, secretory function and absorption.
incompatibilities: ANAT2003: Anatomy of Head, Neck and Trunk
MEDI2103: Alimentary System, Nutrition and Metabolism

title: Cardiovascular, Renal and Respiratory Systems
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will learn about the anatomy and physiology of the cardiovascular, renal, and respiratory systems. In particular, you will learn about the mechanisms that maintain homeostasis within these interconnected systems, while gaining a comprehensive understanding of how these systems respond to physical challenges and learn to relate cardiovascular and respiratory diseases to their underlying pathophysiological pathways. Additionally, you will learn to critically evaluate scientific and medical evidence relating to the cardiovascular, renal and respiratory system to inform hypothesis generation, discussion, and individual decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Describe the anatomical structures of the cardiovascular, renal and respiratory systems. (Scientist and Scholar)
Explain the functions of the cardiovascular, renal and respiratory system, as well as the mechanisms that maintain homeostasis in these coordinated systems. (Scientist and Scholar)
Relate knowledge of the structure and function of the cardiovascular, renal and respiratory system to disease processes. (Scientist and Scholar)
Communicate physiological knowledge professionally. (Practitioner)
incompatibilities: ANAT2003: Anatomy of Head, Neck and Trunk

title: Health, Society and Culture
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will be introduced to the ways health is shaped by social, cultural, and historical factors in Australia. You will explore how people’s experiences of health and wellbeing are influenced by their cultural identity, social position, and access to services. A key focus of the unit is on the health and wellbeing of First Nations peoples, including how colonisation, racism, and social inequalities continue to impact health outcomes today.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and communicate basic information about health and wellbeing in a culturally respectful and inclusive way when engaging with diverse populations. (Professional)
Recognise and discuss how social, cultural, economic, and environmental factors interact to shape health outcomes in diverse communities across Australia. (Citizen)
Explain the historical and ongoing impacts of colonisation, racism, and marginalisation on the health and wellbeing of First Nations peoples. (Practitioner)
Identify and describe key social, cultural, and environmental determinants of health and wellbeing, with a particular focus on the experiences of First Nations peoples. (Scientist and Scholar)

title: Nervous System
syllabus_overview: This unit will provide you with an introductory understanding of the nervous system. This unit integrates both anatomy and physiology allowing you to learn about how the nervous system is organised and communicates information with a particular focus on the production of movement, processing of sensory information, regulation of homeostatic function and the basics of learning and memory. You will also be introduced to drug classes that positively and negatively affect the functioning of the nervous system and the clinical consequences that arise from pathological changes to the nervous system. Key learning activities will include lectures, tutorial and practical sessions.
learning_outcomes: Describe the general organisation of the nervous system and how communication occurs within the nervous system.
Discuss how the nervous system produces movement, processes sensory information, regulates homeostatic function and consolidates learning and memory.
Outline the mechanism of action of specific drug classes that affect the functioning of the nervous system.
Identify how common pathological conditions affect neural control of movement, sensation, homeostatic function and/or learning and memory.
Identify the brain structures critical for movement, sensation, homeostatic function, and learning and memory.

title: Health and Wellbeing across the Lifespan
faculty: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
school: School of Health Sciences and Nursing
syllabus_overview: This unit explores how physical, mental, and social health change throughout life, from infancy to older adulthood. You will learn about the unique health challenges people face at different stages and discover advanced health coaching strategies to address them. By the end of the unit, you will be able to create and assess health interventions that help individuals improve their wellbeing, using evidence-based and culturally sensitive approaches.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of how lifestyle factors influence health outcomes across the lifespan to develop strategies that enhance overall health and wellbeing. (Practitioner)
Create evidence-based, culturally sensitive health coaching interventions that address the unique needs and challenges of individuals at different life stages. (Citizen)

Assess and reflect on the effectiveness of health interventions designed to enhance health outcomes across the lifespan, incorporating ethical considerations and evidence-based practices. (Professional)
Critically examine the key physical, psychological, and social health changes that occur across the human lifespan, drawing on evidence from multiple sources. (Scientist and Scholar)

title: PACE: Professional Practice 3
syllabus_overview: This unit is the capstone unit for the Bachelor of Health Sciences, designed to ensure that you achieve the course learning outcomes and are set up for success. In this unit, you will create and present a comprehensive learning portfolio that showcases the knowledge, skills, and attributes you have developed throughout your studies. You will also apply these competencies in a partner-led project, providing you with the practical experience required to evidence your capabilities as a health scientist. Together, this unit will equip you with the confidence and readiness to enter the workforce as a health scientist, setting you up for the next phase of your career journey.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and synthesise contemporary research findings that underpin current and evolving issues relevant to the study of health. (Scientist and Scholar)
Identify and design innovative solutions to current and emerging health-related problems. (Practitioner)

Demonstrate reflexive and reflective skills that enable selfevaluation, sound ethical judgement to advance personal and professional goals and commit to the self-directed pursuit of ongoing professional development for impact in life beyond University. (Professional)
Identify, advocate for, and adopt strategies that promote health and wellbeing as appropriate to varied contextual factors across a range of settings and in times of uncertainty. (Citizen)
Discuss, apply, and interpret health science knowledge across a range of health-related topics. (Scientist and Scholar)
Explain the importance of maintaining health to society across a diverse range of cultural settings. (Citizen)
Disseminate health-related information to broad consumer groups utilising multiple modes of communication. (Practitioner)
Demonstrate effective interpersonal skills that enable collaborative work both within a team and as a leader. (Professional)

title: Navigating Digital Health Data: Governance, Ethics, Privacy, and Security
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will explore the critical aspects of digital health data management, focusing on governance frameworks, ethical considerations, privacy laws, and security practices. Through a mix of theoretical knowledge and practical application, you will develop the skills necessary to navigate the complexities of digital health environments. By the end of this unit, you will be equipped with the knowledge and skills necessary to navigate the rapidly evolving landscape of digital health.
learning_outcomes: Explain the key governance frameworks and policies that guide the management of digital health data. (Scientist and Scholar)
Critically assess ethical issues related to the collection, storage, and use of health data in digital formats. (Professional)
Demonstrate knowledge of privacy legislation applicable to digital health data, including the implications for healthcare providers and patients. (Scientist and Scholar)
Identify and implement appropriate security measures to protect digital health data from breaches and unauthorised access. (Practitioner)

title: Digital Health System Design
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will explore the principles and methodologies for designing effective digital health systems. You will learn about user-centred design, system integration, and the evaluation of digital health technologies. By completing this unit, you will gain practical skills in creating solutions that improve healthcare delivery, enhance patient engagement, and support health professionals in their workflows.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of integrating various digital health technologies and systems to create cohesive solutions. (Scientist and Scholar)
Assess the performance and effectiveness of digital health systems using appropriate evaluation frameworks. (Citizen)
Effectively present and justify design concepts and solutions to a range of stakeholders, incorporating research findings to support decision-making. (Practitioner)
Apply user-centred design principles to develop digital health systems that meet the needs of diverse stakeholders. (Practitioner)

title: Health Data Analytics
syllabus_overview: This unit will equip you will the skills and knowledge necessary to analyse and interpret health data. You will learn how to apply data analytics techniques to improve healthcare outcomes, enhance patient care, and support evidence-based decision-making in health services. You will explore the various tools and methodologies used in health data analytics, including statistical analysis, predictive modelling, and data visualisation.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the results of data analyses and articulate their implications for clinical practice and health policy. (Scientist and Scholar)
Demonstrate the ability to collect, clean, and analyse health-related data using appropriate analytical methods and tools. (Scientist and Scholar)
Apply and recommend ethical principles and standards relevant to the use of health data, including privacy and security considerations. (Professional)
Effectively communicate analytical findings to a range of stakeholders through various formats. (Practitioner)

title: Research Foundations
syllabus_overview: In this foundation unit, you will examine the framework for research in medicine, health and human science in Australia covering critical topics of ethics, integrity, funding and cultural safety. This unit will showcase the world class research conducted in the faculty, in Macquarie Medical School and the School of Psychological Sciences, in the three departments of Chiropractic, Health Sciences and Linguistics, as well as the Australian Institute of Health Innovation. The faculty has particular research strengths in neurosciences, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, clinical trials, hearing, linguistics, lifespan health and wellbeing and health systems research. In this unit you will explore the key capabilities needed for successful research.
learning_outcomes: Pose effective research questions, and describe key components in research design.
Explain the fundamentals of different research approaches taken in different disciplines.
Critique different methodologies that might be applied to address research questions.
Describe good practice, including ethics, integrity and leadership.
incompatibilities: MEDI7001: Medical Research Foundations - Ethics, Integrity and Practice

title: Research Frontiers
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will develop an advanced conceptual knowledge of breakthrough discoveries relevant to a range of topics within medicine, health and human sciences. You will gain discipline-specific knowledge that will be relevant to your future research career. You will attend seminars and lectures focused on ongoing research projects from the Faculty of Medicine, Health and Human Sciences and from invited speakers from leading national and international research institutes.You will also learn to conduct research, read and critically review seminal research findings that have shaped contemporary thinking, and to disseminate these findings in written and oral form.
learning_outcomes: Apply skills in research literacy and research related information technology.
Synthesise and analyse research information from a wide variety of resources in your discipline
Articulate clear arguments in written and oral form for a variety of audiences.
Reflect on the breadth of research in the disciplines of medicine, health and human sciences
Identify and discuss complex problems and issues in research within your discipline
incompatibilities: MEDI7011: Research Frontiers in Medical Science 1

title: Research Communications
syllabus_overview: This unit aims to equip you with skills to communicate research effectively, and with a heightened appreciation of the relationship between research communications and disciplinary knowledge creation. You will analyse, critique and practise academic communication conventions from different research genres in a variety of modes (written, oral and visual), across disciplines. You will develop communication skills to present a clear and coherent exposition of research concepts to a variety of audiences.
learning_outcomes: Critique research communication approaches used by various disciplines.
Explain the structure and style of various types of research communications for different audiences
Engage with feedback to enhance research communication practice
Effectively utilise written, oral, and visual communications to disseminate research.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Oral presentation, critical review and practice

title: Research Methodology and Analysis
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will explore advanced practice in data analysis related to the research problems faced in your field of study. You will learn about the fundamentals of reproducible science using case studies that illustrate various practices. You will review different research data, and explore best practice in preparing it for reports and publications. You will learn about experimental design and methodology relevant to your research discipline; including data analytics and statistical analysis, and digital tools that support your research.
learning_outcomes: Present clearly articulated analysis of data from your selected research discipline.
Critique and apply theories and methodologies underpinning analytical approaches for advanced research data.
Critically review research methodologies and justify analytical approaches to interpret data.
Explain complex research concepts and ideas using discipline-specific language.

title: Research Practice
syllabus_overview: This unit focuses on providing a first hand experience of performing research and research communication. In this unit, you will gain experience under the supervision of an experienced researcher. Learning activities will include participation in research activities such as assisting in the acquisition, analysis and interpretation of data, participation in research group meetings and journal clubs, and practical experience in research communication. The immersive learning environment within the research activities will provide you with access to discipline-specific expertise, and you will be able to demonstrate the application of the theoretical knowledge obtained in your other learning activities. Through this unit you will develop skills as a researcher and research communicator.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate well-developed judgement, adaptability and accountability in your professional practice as a researcher.
Communicate theoretical and practical knowledge of relevant research concepts and ideas.
Participate in day-to-day research activities and collaborate in discussion centred around research ideas, methods, and data.
Acquire, analyse, and interpret research data in a way suitable for presentation to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Research Project Management
syllabus_overview: In this unit you will review the key stages of a research project, from conception to completion. Topics covered will include: project design and planning; establishing key project contributors; launching a project; managing a project underway; troubleshooting and dealing with change; record keeping; communicating and networking; publishing; and project completion. These topics will be explored in the context of short (1 year) and long (3 year) research projects. In completing this unit, you will develop a clear understanding of how to deliver a research project from start to finish.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate components and deliverables of a project.
Demonstrate skills in communication and self-directed learning.
Apply understanding of project management techniques in selected disciplinary practice.
Describe the coordination of a research project with a diverse multidisciplinary team.
Evaluate best project troubleshooting approaches and the required associated steps.
Describe how to design and deliver a project plan.

title: Advanced Research Practice
syllabus_overview: This unit focuses on the development of a comprehensive research proposal using advanced knowledge, theories and methods required to conduct research in your discipline. Learning activities will include an opportunity to participate in research activities such as assisting in the acquisition, analysis and interpretation of data, participation in research group meetings and journal clubs, and practical experience in research communication. The immersive learning environment of the research activities will provide you with access to discipline-specific expertise, and you will be able to demonstrate the application of the theoretical knowledge obtained in your other learning activities. Through this unit you will further develop skills as a researcher and research communicator.

Communicate relevant research concepts and ideas to specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Apply ethics and integrity frameworks required to conduct responsible, ethical and reflective research in your discipline.
Develop a research proposal using advanced knowledge, theories and methods required to conduct research in your discipline.

title: Researcher Reflective Practice and Professional Development
syllabus_overview: This unit provides you with the opportunity to develop a wide range of bespoke research and professional skills that support and enhance both research and researcher career development. Working with a mentor, you will curate your professional development from a range of flexible learning activities, tailoring your learning to your research project(s) and professional goals. Professional development opportunities may include but are not limited to: digital research skills; data management; tools and software training; publishing, presenting and communicating research; project management; mentoring and coaching; research leadership, and more. This unit will equip you with the ability to identify and reflect upon your unique strengths and transferable skills developed throughout your research and related professional experiences, as well as the skills and mindsets to plan and accomplish continuous future development. Through the skills and attributes obtained in this unit, you will enhance your ability to confidently undertake research and make meaningful and impactful contributions in research, industry and the community.

Communicate relevant research concepts and ideas to specialist and non-specialist audiences through the development of reflective practice and evidence of professional development.

Demonstrate reflexivity, judgement, adaptability and accountability in your professional practice as a researcher.
Evaluate discipline-specific concepts and practices to identify and contextualise transferable skills as they apply to researchers and research-related careers.

title: Human Structure and Function
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces key concepts in human anatomy and physiology, focusing on how the body is structured and how it works. You will explore the major body systems and how they interact, giving you a strong foundation for further study in health sciences. The unit highlights the connections between body systems, their role in keeping the body in balance, and how to use anatomical and physiological terms to accurately describe different parts of the body and their function.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate correct use of anatomical and physiological terms when describing body structures and their functions. (Scientist and Scholar)
Explain the interrelationships between body systems and their role in maintaining homeostasis. (Scientist and Scholar)
Describe the structure and function of the major body systems. (Scientist and Scholar)

title: Professional Practice 1
syllabus_overview: This unit will provide you with a thorough introduction to the essential capabilities required for a career in health or human sciences, emphasising key concepts of professionalism, including self-reflection, effective communication, and teamwork. Through engaging interactive tutorials, online modules, and peer engagement, you will develop critical learning strategies, enhance your collaborative abilities, and refine your communication skills. These foundational capabilities prepare you to become a reflective and effective professional, equipped with the tools needed to be a life-long learner and succeed in the broad health or human sciences field.
learning_outcomes: Develop learning techniques to effectively manage academic tasks and address learning challenges specific to the health sciences discipline. (Scientist and Scholar)
Clearly and professionally convey information using various communication techniques appropriate to both an individual and group setting. (Practitioner)

title: Evidence-Based Practice in Health
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will learn how to use research to make informed decisions in healthcare. You will develop the practical skills needed to apply evidence-based approaches to real health issues, while considering different cultural needs. By the end of the unit, you will know how to assess research, apply solutions based on evidence, and work ethically and responsibly.

title: Health Systems
syllabus_overview: This unit offers an introductory overview of the Australian healthcare system, delving into its structure, functions, and the roles of various stakeholders. You will explore how healthcare is delivered, funded, and regulated, and examine the challenges facing the system. By the end of the unit, you will be equipped to analyse the current healthcare landscape in Australia and understand its implications for both health care professionals and patients.

Evaluate the health disparities experienced by various minority groups and the role of specialised services in providing culturally sensitive care. (Citizen)

Identify and communicate the key aspects of funding mechanisms, policy frameworks, and stakeholder roles within the Australian healthcare system. (Practitioner)

title: Lifestyle Factors for Health and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This unit explores how a range of lifestyle choices shape overall health and wellbeing. You will learn about factors such as sleep, nutrition, and physical activity, and how they interact to influence both personal and community health. Through evidence-based approaches, you will discover practical ways to improve daily habits and understand how these factors help prevent and manage chronic diseases. This unit lays the groundwork for further study in health sciences and equips you with valuable skills for managing your own health as well as a career in health.
learning_outcomes: Describe the interrelationship between key lifestyle factors and their influence on overall health and wellbeing. (Capability 1: Scientist and Scholar)
Assess the impact of lifestyle choices on health outcomes at the individual and community level. (Capability 3: Citizen)

title: Health, Society and Culture
syllabus_overview: In this unit, you will be introduced to the ways health is shaped by social, cultural, and historical factors in Australia. You will explore how people’s experiences of health and wellbeing are influenced by their cultural identity, social position, and access to services. A key focus of the unit is on the health and wellbeing of First Nations peoples, including how colonisation, racism, and social inequalities continue to impact health outcomes today.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and communicate basic information about health and wellbeing in a culturally respectful and inclusive way when engaging with diverse populations. (Professional)
Recognise and discuss how social, cultural, economic, and environmental factors interact to shape health outcomes in diverse communities across Australia. (Citizen)

You will consider how research is designed and interpreted, gaining an appreciation of how evidence informs psychological knowledge and practice. You will also build skills in communicating psychological concepts to different audiences and reflect on how psychological principles can be applied ethically and with cultural awareness in diverse health and clinical contexts.

title: Forging the West
syllabus_overview: Learn about the origins of the modern world order while developing fundamental skills of historical analysis. In 1215 CE, a Mongol army led by Genghis Khan conquered the Chinese city of Zongdhu (present-day Beijing), creating the basis for the largest contiguous land empire in human history. That same year, leaders of the Latin Church met for the Fourth Lateran Council in Rome at the other end of Eurasia, establishing western European Christian doctrine for three centuries. These civilizations soon came into contact as the Mongol Empire enabled commerce and cultural exchange between east and west Eurasia. This unit explores how the complex network of connections that linked Europe and the wider world between the High Middle Ages and the eve of the modern era helped to create the particular society and culture that we today frequently refer to as “the West.” We focus on the historical contingency of this creation and the ways that both European and non-European influences and factors forged the idea of the West. From medieval encounters between Christianity and Islam to eighteenth-century encounters between Pacific Islanders and Europeans, from the thirteenth-century Eurasian economic world system to the global economy that emerged, we explore the transformation of the premodern world. The unit considers these processes from both European and non-European perspectives
learning_outcomes: Pose and investigate questions of a variety of historical sources, locating them in their appropriate contexts.
Synthesise primary and secondary sources to develop clear, specific, evidence-based arguments in response to historical questions.
Explain the ways in which religion, trade, and empire connected the premodern world.
Analyse and assess the impact that various events, movements and ideas had on the creation of the premodern world, producing a complex picture of this world.
incompatibilities: MHIX1001: Forging the West: A World History of Europe, 1215-1788

title: Misconceptions in the Modern World
syllabus_overview: This unit will introduce you to the history and philosophy of science and assist in the development of your critical thinking skills, with a focus on applications in health and human sciences. You will be challenged to question openly the accuracy of mainstream information and the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in enabling misconceptions. You will develop basic AI literacy skills, evaluate health and human science claims, and become equipped to communicate health information accurately and effectively. This unit combines theoretical learning with practical activities that will engage you in real-world health and human science challenges.

Reflect on the ethical and societal impacts of disseminating inaccurate health and human science information and perpetuating misconceptions. (Capability 4: Professional)

Explain how AI technologies can be used to advance health and human science and describe the potential societal risks and benefits AI poses for accurate health and human science information. (Capability 3: Citizen)

incompatibilities: MHHS1008: Misconceptions in the Modern World

title: Making the Modern World
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces students to foundational skills and concepts in the study of modern history from the late eighteenth century. Students will traverse the world from 1789 to 2001 looking closely at the role of revolution and the emergence of the nation-state, as well as the cost to humans and the natural world of economic growth and colonisation. Beginning with the French Revolution, the unit investigates conflict and change in the quest for equality and citizenship, telling the story of democratic aspirations in the modern world, including competing visions of modernity. It considers those excluded along with the new forms of solidarity and enmity created against the backdrop of rapid industrialisation, capitalism and environmental change. Students will build a foundational chronology of the modern world and develop skills such as critical and analytical thinking, effective communication and empathy. Students will build a foundational chronology of the modern world and develop skills such as critical and analytical thinking, effective communication and empathy.
learning_outcomes: Identify core issues and problems in building historical knowledge.
Construct a foundational chronological framework of significant major modern historical developments.
Locate and organise historical information from a range of sources to support evidence-based arguments and responsible scholarly practice.
Communicate scholarly arguments in response to historical questions, drawing upon primary and secondary sources.
incompatibilities: MHIS1002: Revolutions, Nationalism and Exploitation in the Modern World 1789-2001

title: Merchants, Markets, and Globalisation
syllabus_overview: Globalisation is older than we think. In the European Middle Ages, a network of trade routes connected the Afro-Eurasian landmass, which made possible the extensive travels of Italian merchant Marco Polo and Moroccan scholar Ibn Battuta. In the sixteenth century, these networks expanded to include the Americas, creating the first global economy. This unit traces the long history of global capitalism from its medieval origins to the data-driven on-line commerce of the twenty-first century. It explores how commerce and exchange have developed over the past millennium, considering the ideas, commodities, and political forces that have facilitated and impeded trade. It examines the social, cultural, and environmental impacts of global capitalism. This unit explains how the world economy we live today took shape and why it operates the way that it does.
learning_outcomes: Analyse a variety of historical sources, including visual materials, to comprehend and assess the development of the global economy from the Middle Ages to the twenty-first century.
Collaborate in group discussions to develop persuasive historical reasoning and deepen understanding of contested historical narratives.
Engage with major historiographical debates in the field in order to develop clear, specific, evidence-based arguments in response to historical questions.
Design and deliver an independent project using appropriate historical methods, communicating ideas and historical arguments in an engaging, concise and accessible style.
incompatibilities: MHIS2004: Capitalism in World History: From the Silk Roads to Amazon

title: Encountering the Middle Ages
syllabus_overview: This unit will explore the culture, politics and religion of the medieval period. It considers Byzantium, the establishment of Islam and the Islamic world, and the emergence of Latin Christendom in western Europe. Each of these ‘new’ societies established novel forms of political organisation and social structure, embedded in their religious culture. This unit will explore these changes by consideration of a diversity of visual and written sources. Students will also be exposed to scholarly debates relevant to these fields. Some historians argue that the medieval period provides the foundation for modernity, while others suggest that we should encounter the Middle Ages as other to the present. Students will engage with these debates to develop advanced skills in historiography, as well as to build capacity in their knowledge of the pre-modern past.
learning_outcomes: Identify the key political, religious, and cultural developments of the medieval period across Byzantium, the Islamic world, and Latin Christendom.
Evaluate and synthesise differing scholarly interpretations of medieval history to identify historiographical trends and debates.
Analyse and interpret a diverse range of medieval primary sources, including written and visual materials, within their historical contexts.
Reflect critically on the relationship between the medieval past and the modern world, assessing the relevance and implications of historical figures, ideas, and events.

AHIX2130: Byzantium in the Age of the Emperors

title: Despots and Democracy
syllabus_overview: This unit explores the dynamic and often turbulent relationship between autocracy and democratic governance across the 19th and 20th centuries. From the rise of nationalist despots and imperial rulers to the emergence and evolution of modern democratic states, students will examine how different regimes consolidated power, legitimized authority, and responded to social and political movements challenging their rule. Through comparative and thematic Through comparative and thematic approaches, students will analyze the role of ideology, violence, propaganda, revolution, and resistance in shaping political life. The unit will also investigate the global forces—industrialization, imperialism, war, decolonization, and globalization—that influenced transitions between despotism and democracy.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse primary and secondary historical sources to assess how power is constructed, maintained, and contested.
Engage with and interpret major historiographical debates, related to despotism, democracy, and political transitions in modern history.
Construct and communicate a well-supported historical argument in written form, demonstrating analytical thinking, source evaluation, and coherent structure.
Compare and evaluate different political systems and their responses to movements for reform, revolution, and resistance.
incompatibilities: MHIS2001: Between Hope and Despair: A History of Human Rights
MHIX2001: A History of Human Rights

title: Screening the Past: History on Film and Television
syllabus_overview: Recent surveys of popular historical awareness have demonstrated that most people find out about the past from film and television, yet visual histories are often criticised for the ways they present the past. This unit will consider the limitations and possibilities of history on screen. Do filmic histories represent a more 'authentic' engagement with the past, or do they peddle false versions of history to a gullible public? How might we read historical films and television programs carefully and critically to understand diverse historical interpretations? This unit will develop student's understandings of the critical study of history on film, examining the ways that all historical texts (including films) make arguments about the past. The unit will examine cinematic and televisual representations of Australian, American and British histories.
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply a critical vocabulary for the analysis of film and televisual materials as primary sources.
Locate historical films and television programs within the context of their production.
Successfully undertake independent primary and secondary historical research.
Conceptualise and create an original research project by presenting a coherent historical argument that is situated in the relevant historiography.
Demonstrate understanding of the ways that films and television programs produce interpretations of the past.
incompatibilities: MHIX3030: Screening the Past: History on Film and Television
PBHS1101: Screening the Past: History on Film and Television
PBHX1101: Screening the Past: History on Film and Television

title: Who the Bloody Hell Are We?: Story and Citizenship in Australian History
syllabus_overview: Ideas about Australian identity have always been expressed and contested in popular culture. These stories of ‘us’ have also meant that some people are seen to belong, and others are excluded from the full exercise of citizenship. This unit will examine Australian history through an examination of 10 key moments when the nation and its citizens were re-imagined in films, songs, novels, poetry, advertisements, sporting contests and plays. Each week we will examine a key turning point in Australian history and the popular culture that was produced to grapple with its consequences. When and why did the bushman become a central figure in the Australian imagination? How did ‘Muriel’s Wedding’ reimagine mateship in the wake of feminist protest? In what ways did advertisements featuring Rhonda and Ketut envisage the relationship between Australia and Asia? Students who complete this unit will develop a critical understanding of the relationship between storytelling and citizenship, master a chronology of the struggles over citizenship that shaped twentieth century Australian political history, and engage widely with the cultural institutions and archives in which our national memory is stored. They will also engage in a wide variety of historical research, classroom debate, and develop an original research topic to investigate. If you have already studied some Australian history, the unit offers a fresh perspective. It will be particularly useful for students who are intending to teach Australian history in schools.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively in a range of written forms.
Conceptualise and create an original research project by presenting a coherent historical argument that is situated in the relevant historiography
Understand the ways that Australian culture articulates ideas about Australian citizenship, and explain how these ideas have changed over time.
Analyse different kinds of historical evidence, including visual and textual sources.

title: War and Peace in World History
syllabus_overview: While war can be viewed purely in terms of military strategy and through the lens of advancing armies, it also has wider social, economic and cultural meanings that situate men and women as historical actors in the formation of cultures and societies and the construction of new world orders. We explore the cultural frameworks that give wars their meaning, the different terms under which peace has been forged and practiced, and the long history of debates about lawful and unlawful warfare. We pay particular attention to how ideas of men and masculinity are shaped by war, to the colonial context of much international conflict and to the ways that wars become stories through memorialisation. This unit takes a ‘case study’ approach, examining 4 major conflicts to develop deep historical knowledge about major wars and their resolutions as well as explore critical frameworks to robustly historicise war and peace making.
learning_outcomes: Apply digital humanities methods and tools to research, interpret, and present histories of war and peace using relevant digital sources.
Develop and communicate historical arguments through effective use of primary and secondary sources, demonstrating critical thinking and an awareness of historiographical debates.
Identify and explain key historical conflicts and peace processes in global history, including their political, cultural, and ideological foundations.
Evaluate how war has shaped national, imperial, and collective memory across different historical and geographical contexts.
incompatibilities: MHIX3301: War and Peace in World History

title: From the Beats to the Bachelorette: A History of Popular Culture since 1945
syllabus_overview: What can we learn about the past when we examine it through the lens of popular culture? This unit traces a history of popular culture in the United States of America and Australia from the 1950s to the present, exploring the ways that popular culture can magnify and reflect changing ideas about race, class, gender, and ideology. We will examine the impact of new technologies, moral panics over popular culture, and whether popular culture constituted a form of cultural citizenship. Film, television, music and other media are used in this unit to evoke seminal moments in the history of popular culture and students are encouraged to explore these non-discursive forms as primary sources. Students are also encouraged to consider the reception of popular culture by audiences and to think about their own experience of popular culture historically. This unit will be of particular interest to students in media, education, and cultural studies, as well as history.
learning_outcomes: Be able to identify and analyse key developments in the history of popular culture since 1945
Locate, read, and analyse different kinds of historical evidence (primary sources), including visual and textual sources
Devise and answer research questions drawing on primary and secondary evidence
Communicate thoughtfully in classroom discussions, and in a range of written forms
Identify key arguments in secondary source materials and apply them in your own historical arguments

Analyse selected examples of popular culture produced since 1945 in their historical contexts, and describe the ways these examples, relate to, and reflect, broader, social, cultural, and political trends

title: Histories of Gender and Sexuality
syllabus_overview: Sexuality and gender are two of the oldest forces shaping human experience. This unit examines histories of gender and sexuality in the modern world, interrogating the ways that gender and sexuality have been constructed, regulated, and represented over time, while also asking how these histories have been written, debated, and theorised. Students will focus on historiographical debates and the methodological questions that have shaped gender history: how have historians approached the study of gender and sexuality? What theoretical frameworks have shaped the field? And how do archives, silences, and power dynamics affect the writing of these histories? Students will gain an understanding of gender and sexuality as historical categories and knowledge of the ways in which gender and sexuality have helped to shape significant intellectual, political and social developments in history. Students will develop understandings of the complexity of gender and sexuality in the past, in order to develop critical tools for the analysis of sex and gender in the present.

Evaluate historiographical debates and methodological approaches to the history of gender and sexuality, including the impact of archives, silences, and power dynamics on historical narratives.
Reflect on key concepts and debates in the history of gender and sexuality to develop critical tools for analysing gender and sexuality in both past and present contexts.
Critically analyse the ways gender and sexuality have been constructed, regulated, and represented across diverse historical contexts in the modern world.

title: Human Rights and Social Change
syllabus_overview: What are human rights? How have they evolved and what is the political and cultural investment in them? How and why does a concept defined by hope and aspiration, promising human rights and freedoms, remain elusive and problematic in theory and practice? We will explore this history through social movements and legal systems, as well as politics, philosophy and rights discourses. We consider the personal and collective stories of human rights and explore key moments in their development from Magna Carta to Indigenous self-determination and climate change. The unit deepens and complicates understandings of modernity . In addition, it provides crucial historical background, context and terminology for students interested in careers in international law, foreign aid, global politics and humanitarian organisations.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the historical development of human rights across key moments, movements, and legal frameworks, from early charters to contemporary global issues.
Interrogate archival sources to assess their potential and limitations in constructing histories of human rights and identifying voices often excluded from official narratives.
Evaluate the cultural, political, and philosophical dimensions of human rights discourse, including the tensions between theory and practice.
Create persuasive, evidence-based resources that engage critically with historical materials to advocate for social change and the uptake of specific human rights in local and global contexts.

Evaluate and synthesise differing scholarly interpretations of medieval history to identify historiographical trends and debates.
Identify the key political, religious, and cultural developments of the medieval period across Byzantium, the Islamic world, and Latin Christendom.
incompatibilities: MHIS2007: From Charlemagne to Game of Thrones: The Middle Ages Then and Now
MHIX2007: From Charlemagne to Game of Thrones: The Middle Ages Then and Now
AHIS2130: Byzantium in the Age of the Emperors
AHIX2130: Byzantium in the Age of the Emperors

title: Merchants, Markets, and Globalisation
syllabus_overview: Globalisation is older than we think. In the European Middle Ages, a network of trade routes connected the Afro-Eurasian landmass, which made possible the extensive travels of Italian merchant Marco Polo and Moroccan scholar Ibn Battuta. In the sixteenth century, these networks expanded to include the Americas, creating the first global economy. This unit traces the long history of global capitalism from its medieval origins to the data-driven on-line commerce of the twenty-first century. It explores how commerce and exchange have developed over the past millennium, considering the ideas, commodities, and political forces that have facilitated and impeded trade. It examines the social, cultural, and environmental impacts of global capitalism. This unit explains how the world economy we live today took shape and why it operates the way that it does.
learning_outcomes: Design and deliver an independent project using appropriate historical methods, communicating ideas and historical arguments in an engaging, concise and accessible style.
Analyse a variety of historical sources, including visual materials, to comprehend and assess the development of the global economy from the Middle Ages to the twenty-first century.
Collaborate in group discussions to develop persuasive historical reasoning and deepen understanding of contested historical narratives.
Engage with major historiographical debates in the field in order to develop clear, specific, evidence-based arguments in response to historical questions.

title: Despots and Democracy
syllabus_overview: This unit explores the dynamic and often turbulent relationship between autocracy and democratic governance across the 19th and 20th centuries. From the rise of nationalist despots and imperial rulers to the emergence and evolution of modern democratic states, students will examine how different regimes consolidated power, legitimized authority, and responded to social and political movements challenging their rule. Through comparative and thematic Through comparative and thematic approaches, students will analyze the role of ideology, violence, propaganda, revolution, and resistance in shaping political life. The unit will also investigate the global forces—industrialization, imperialism, war, decolonization, and globalization—that influenced transitions between despotism and democracy.
learning_outcomes: Construct and communicate a well-supported historical argument in written form, demonstrating analytical thinking, source evaluation, and coherent structure.
Engage with and interpret major historiographical debates, related to despotism, democracy, and political transitions in modern history.
Critically analyse primary and secondary historical sources to assess how power is constructed, maintained, and contested.
Compare and evaluate different political systems and their responses to movements for reform, revolution, and resistance.

title: From the Beats to the Bachelorette: Popular Culture Since the 1950s
syllabus_overview: What can we learn about the past when we examine it through the lens of popular culture? This unit traces a history of popular culture in the United States of America and Australia from the 1950s to the present, exploring the ways that popular culture can magnify and reflect changing ideas about race, class, gender, and ideology. We will examine the impact of new technologies, moral panics over popular culture, and whether popular culture constituted a form of cultural citizenship. Film, television, music and other media are used in this unit to evoke seminal moments in the history of popular culture and students are encouraged to explore these non-discursive forms as primary sources. Students are also encouraged to consider the reception of popular culture by audiences and to think about their own experience of popular culture historically. This unit will be of particular interest to students in media, education, and cultural studies, as well as history.
learning_outcomes: Locate, read, and analyse different kinds of historical evidence (primary sources), including visual and textual sources
Devise and answer research questions drawing on primary and secondary evidence
Identify key arguments in secondary source materials and apply them in your own historical arguments
Communicate thoughtfully in classroom discussions, and in a range of written forms

Analyse selected examples of popular culture produced since 1945 in their historical contexts, and describe the ways these examples, relate to, and reflect, broader, social, cultural, and political trends
Be able to identify and analyse key developments in the history of popular culture since 1945
incompatibilities: MHIS3065: From the Beats to the Bachelorette: Popular Culture Since the 1950s

title: Screening the Past: History on Film and Television
syllabus_overview: Recent surveys of popular historical awareness have demonstrated that most people find out about the past from film and television, yet visual histories are often criticised for the ways they present the past. This unit will consider the limitations and possibilities of history on screen. Do filmic histories represent a more 'authentic' engagement with the past, or do they peddle false versions of history to a gullible public? How might we read historical films and television programs carefully and critically to understand diverse historical interpretations? This unit will develop student's understandings of the critical study of history on film, examining the ways that all historical texts (including films) make arguments about the past. The unit will examine cinematic and televisual representations of Australian, American and British histories.
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply a critical vocabulary for the analysis of film and televisual materials as primary sources.
Conceptualise and create an original research project by presenting a coherent historical argument that is situated in the relevant historiography.
Successfully undertake independent primary and secondary historical research.
Locate historical films and television programs within the context of their production.
Demonstrate understanding of the ways that films and television programs produce interpretations of the past.
incompatibilities: MHIS3030: Screening the Past: History on Film and Television
PBHS1101: Screening the Past: History on Film and Television
PBHX1101: Screening the Past: History on Film and Television

title: Who the Bloody Hell Are We? Story and Citizenship in Australian History
syllabus_overview: Ideas about Australian identity have always been expressed and contested in popular culture. These stories of ‘us’ have also meant that some people are seen to belong, and others are excluded from the full exercise of citizenship. This unit will examine Australian history through an examination of 10 key moments when the nation and its citizens were re-imagined in films, songs, novels, poetry, advertisements, sporting contests and plays. Each week we will examine a key turning point in Australian history and the popular culture that was produced to grapple with its consequences. When and why did the bushman become a central figure in the Australian imagination? How did ‘Muriel’s Wedding’ reimagine mateship in the wake of feminist protest? In what ways did advertisements featuring Rhonda and Ketut envisage the relationship between Australia and Asia? Students who complete this unit will develop a critical understanding of the relationship between storytelling and citizenship, master a chronology of the struggles over citizenship that shaped twentieth century Australian political history, and engage widely with the cultural institutions and archives in which our national memory is stored. They will also engage in a wide variety of historical research, classroom debate, and develop an original research topic to investigate. If you have already studied some Australian history, the unit offers a fresh perspective. It will be particularly useful for students who are intending to teach Australian history in schools.
learning_outcomes: Understand the ways that Australian culture articulates ideas about Australian citizenship, and explain how these ideas have changed over time.
Communicate effectively in a range of written forms.
Analyse different kinds of historical evidence, including visual and textual sources.
Conceptualise and create an original research project by presenting a coherent historical argument that is situated in the relevant historiography

title: War and Peace in World History
syllabus_overview: While war can be viewed purely in terms of military strategy and through the lens of advancing armies, it also has wider social, economic and cultural meanings that situate men and women as historical actors in the formation of cultures and societies and the construction of new world orders. We explore the cultural frameworks that give wars their meaning, the different terms under which peace has been forged and practiced, and the long history of debates about lawful and unlawful warfare. We pay particular attention to how ideas of men and masculinity are shaped by war, to the colonial context of much international conflict and to the ways that wars become stories through memorialisation. This unit takes a ‘case study’ approach, examining 4 major conflicts to develop deep historical knowledge about major wars and their resolutions as well as explore critical frameworks to robustly historicise war and peace making.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate how war has shaped national, imperial, and collective memory across different historical and geographical contexts.
Apply digital humanities methods and tools to research, interpret, and present histories of war and peace using relevant digital sources.
Identify and explain key historical conflicts and peace processes in global history, including their political, cultural, and ideological foundations.
Develop and communicate historical arguments through effective use of primary and secondary sources, demonstrating critical thinking and an awareness of historiographical debates.
incompatibilities: MHIS3301: War and Peace in World History

title: Histories of Gender and Sexuality
syllabus_overview: Sexuality and gender are two of the oldest forces shaping human experience. This unit examines histories of gender and sexuality in the modern world, interrogating the ways that gender and sexuality have been constructed, regulated, and represented over time, while also asking how these histories have been written, debated, and theorised. Students will focus on historiographical debates and the methodological questions that have shaped gender history: how have historians approached the study of gender and sexuality? What theoretical frameworks have shaped the field? And how do archives, silences, and power dynamics affect the writing of these histories? Students will gain an understanding of gender and sexuality as historical categories and knowledge of the ways in which gender and sexuality have helped to shape significant intellectual, political and social developments in history. Students will develop understandings of the complexity of gender and sexuality in the past, in order to develop critical tools for the analysis of sex and gender in the present.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate historiographical debates and methodological approaches to the history of gender and sexuality, including the impact of archives, silences, and power dynamics on historical narratives.
Apply theoretical frameworks to interpret primary and secondary sources with a gendered lens and construct well-supported historical arguments.
Reflect on key concepts and debates in the history of gender and sexuality to develop critical tools for analysing gender and sexuality in both past and present contexts.
Critically analyse the ways gender and sexuality have been constructed, regulated, and represented across diverse historical contexts in the modern world.
incompatibilities: MHIS3302: Histories of Gender and Sexuality

title: Human Rights and Social Change
syllabus_overview: What are human rights? How have they evolved and what is the political and cultural investment in them? How and why does a concept defined by hope and aspiration, promising human rights and freedoms, remain elusive and problematic in theory and practice? We will explore this history through social movements and legal systems, as well as politics, philosophy and rights discourses. We consider the personal and collective stories of human rights and explore key moments in their development from Magna Carta to Indigenous self-determination and climate change. The unit deepens and complicates understandings of modernity . In addition, it provides crucial historical background, context and terminology for students interested in careers in international law, foreign aid, global politics and humanitarian organisations.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the historical development of human rights across key moments, movements, and legal frameworks, from early charters to contemporary global issues.
Interrogate archival sources to assess their potential and limitations in constructing histories of human rights and identifying voices often excluded from official narratives.
Evaluate the cultural, political, and philosophical dimensions of human rights discourse, including the tensions between theory and practice.
Create persuasive, evidence-based resources that engage critically with historical materials to advocate for social change and the uptake of specific human rights in local and global contexts.
incompatibilities: MHIS3303: Human Rights and Social Change

title: Marketing and Value Creation
syllabus_overview: This unit focuses on the fundamentals of marketing in any organisation and how to create value for the customer offering. Students learn how to understand the relationship between the organisation and the customer and how to develop strategies to create value. Students will learn the fundamental skills of marketing by applying these skills through practical workshops on a range of real-world case studies. Students will learn skills on how to present themselves and work in collaboration with others.
learning_outcomes: Use a variety of tools to understand the customer, and create value through marketing efforts.
Apply marketing concepts, frameworks and theories to a range of real world scenarios.
Understand fundamentals of marketing, concepts, frameworks and theories.
Communicate marketing solutions to a range of scenarios in a collaborative environment.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Skills development: Writing for social media

title: Consumer Behaviour
syllabus_overview: An important aspect of marketing is to understand the heart and mind of consumers. Understanding why consumers think, feel and act the way that they do assists businesses in making strategic, sustainable and ethical marketing decisions. This unit develops students’ knowledge about how to understand, interpret and influence consumers’ behaviour. Students gain theoretical knowledge of the internal, psychological processes and external, environmental factors influencing consumer behaviour. Students learn about consumer needs and values, how consumers perceive products and brands, ways to measure attitudes and effect attitude change, how and why consumers decide to buy (or not buy), and the importance of culture and reference group influences. By the end of this unit, students have a much deeper and richer appreciation of how consumption not only affects our lives but also how our actions influence the way that we feel about ourselves and about one another.
learning_outcomes: Apply consumer behaviour theory to develop solutions to consumption decisions acknowledging ethical implications for society.
Identify and articulate a range of external and internal influences on consumer behaviour.
Critically analyse and apply consumer behaviour theory to real-world consumption experiences.

title: Marketing Research
syllabus_overview: Marketing research empowers companies by offering deep insights about consumers and markets. It assists organizations to identify potential issues, explore opportunities in the market, and make strategic evidenced-based decisions that develop and sustain their competitiveness. This unit equips students with knowledge about marketing research principles, techniques, and tools. The focus of the unit is on developing students’ skills to design and implement quantitative and qualitative research projects exploring real-world market issues and opportunities. Students will also learn how to apply market research knowledge and skills to interpret research results and develop recommendations to facilitate evidence-based marketing decisions.
learning_outcomes: Apply market research knowledge and skills to interpret research results and communicate results and recommendations in a professional manner
Design and apply qualitative and quantitative research to explore real-world market issues and opportunities, individually and/or in collaboration
Evaluate marketing research principles, techniques, and tools

title: Integrated Marketing Communications
syllabus_overview: The ability to effectively communicate and persuade consumers is a major challenge facing marketers. Aside from clutter, consumers are also getting busier. The rise of social media also means that consumers are now more subtly influenced by their friends, and with the rise in multi-channel marketing, consumers expect a seamless experience when interacting with organisations. Being able to communicate the right message to the right people at the right time, using the right channels in an integrated fashion, is crucial to the success of any marketing communications. This unit develops students’ knowledge of the principles and practices of integrated marketing communications. It covers planning processes, tools of marketing communications, creativity and media planning, among others. Students gain knowledge about developing and implementing effective integrated marketing communications campaigns.
learning_outcomes: Develop an effective integrated marketing communications plan and professionally communicate it to the appropriate audience.
Employ critical thinking techniques to solve marketing communications problems, individually and/or in collaboration
Identify and define key terms, concepts, frameworks and models of marketing communications.

title: Marketing Management
syllabus_overview: In competitive business environments, developing and managing superior value offerings for customers is vital. Managing the marketing offering of a firm is central to market success. To that end, practitioners need to own a set of skills and be able to utilise a mix of tools to target and satisfy their consumers’ needs. This unit develops students’ knowledge and skills to identify target markets, shape a product mix, deliver value to target markets through a communication mix, identify distribution channels, and formulate a pricing mix. Students develop skills of setting objectives, identifying problems, identifying and evaluating alternatives, and implementing an optimal decision.
learning_outcomes: Identify and discuss marketing concepts, individually and in collaboration.
Critically analyse and communicate marketing management problems and opportunities.
Apply and communicate actionable solutions to identify opportunities and solve marketing problems.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Professional practice: Case study analysis and solutions

title: Marketing Technologies
syllabus_overview: The field of marketing is becoming more technology and data-driven. Companies are increasingly demanding marketing talents who possess the ability to navigate data and harness digital touchpoints in creating a personalised brand and user experience. This unit develops students' knowledge on the role of customer data, marketing automation, and intelligent workflow design in uncovering marketing insights, optimising the marketing mix, and facilitating greater marketing agility. This unit bridges the gap between marketing and technology, and develops students’ knowledge of technology platforms, skills in data visualization and storytelling, analytical thinking and problem solving, and understanding of digital-sustainable marketing strategy.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and interpret marketing practices to generate actionable insights through the use of marketing technology tools.
Critically evaluate the capacity of data and technology to foster sustainable marketing practices.
Identify and explain the role of technology and data in enhancing marketing strategies.

title: Qualitative Insights
syllabus_overview: Qualitative insights provide organisations with an in-depth perspective of emerging market trends and novel consumer behaviours. Organisations use qualitative insights to better engage and deliver value to their customers, identify new opportunities and fuel their competitive advantage. This unit equips students with knowledge of the role, theory and methods used in qualitative research. Students will develop skills in qualitative research design, data collection and analysis, including the use of different software packages. Students will also learn how to interpret and translate results to deliver strategic insights, and effectively deliver their findings through both oral and written communication.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate global sustainable thinking to create coherent and theoretically rigorous arguments to address marketing problems.
Apply qualitative research skills, analytic techniques, and narrative structures individually and/or in collaboration, to derive and communicate marketing and consumer insights.
Critically evaluate qualitative approaches, theories, and storytelling frameworks to develop meaningful, insight driven interpretations.

title: Business to Business Marketing
syllabus_overview: Business-to-business markets are the unseen engines powering the global economy. They are vast, often dwarfing consumer markets in terms of complexity, size, and value. Every consumer product, from your smartphone to your sneakers, is the result of countless business-to-business transactions. Understanding these markets is crucial to understanding the business world itself. In this unit, students learn about key challenges surrounding business-to-business marketing, with a focus on relationship building, joint problem solving, and creating value in complex supply chains. This unit develops students’ knowledge and skills in managing multiple stakeholders, navigating long sales cycles, and implementing large-scale solutions. By completing this unit, students will be well-prepared for exciting career opportunities in the business-to-business market that offer immense satisfaction and growth potential.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the theories and concepts underpinning Business-to-Business Marketing, individually and/or in collaboration.
Analyse business-to-business markets to identify threats/opportunities.
Identify and apply theoretically-grounded solutions to business-to-business marketing problems.

title: Marketing Strategy
syllabus_overview: Marketing strategy is fundamental to business success. Marketing strategy is what guides the development and delivery of the firms’ value offering. Marketing strategy outlines a company’s overall plan to reach, communicate with, and turn people into customers. Marketing strategy contains key messages of value propositions that a company wishes to deliver to the market. In this unit students learn how to apply tools and concepts that enable marketing strategies to be developed, evaluated and implemented. The unit focuses on the analysis process: identifying information needs, acquiring the necessary information, interpreting it, and using it as the basis for business recommendations.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the theoretical and conceptual underpinnings of marketing strategies.
Develop and apply competitive marketing strategies, individually and in collaboration.
Employ problem solving skills to develop and communicate solutions for a range of marketing strategy situations.

title: Services Marketing
syllabus_overview: In competitive service markets, offering consistent quality and satisfying services are key challenges. These challenges drive intangibility, heterogeneity, credence qualities and high similarity among competing service offerings. Because of the nature of services, service marketers have to adopt strategies to market their service offerings which are different from tangible goods. There is a growing range of touchpoints, where customers experience service marketing techniques. Therefore, services marketers require a deep understanding of issues such as service design and delivery, service quality measurement and internal marketing. The focus of this unit is on developing students’ knowledge of the specific characteristics of service offerings and service markets. Students will critically analyse and evaluate service offerings and service delivery processes with a focus on creating strategic options to improve service quality, satisfaction, firm performance and brand services competitively.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and justify different strategic options to improve collaboration, service quality, customer satisfaction and firm performance.
Evaluate service marketing theories to solve services problems and communicate your solutions.
Critique and explain the specific characteristics of service offerings and service markets.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Skills development: Reflecting on services marketing
Professional practice: Evaluation of service performance
Professional practice: Service opportunities and challenges

title: PACE: Marketing Project
syllabus_overview: Today, the competitive business world needs people who can bridge the gap between theory and practice. Businesses need marketers who can integrate their knowledge and consolidate their skills, essential in designing and implementing marketing research projects to understand market behaviour and develop useful marketing strategies. This unit develops students’ ability to apply marketing theory to practice through solving a marketing problem for a Client Partner. This unit focuses on identifying factors which influence the competitive positioning of a firm within an industry and to achieve an ethical, socially responsible, and sustainable competitive advantage. Visit Employability Connect for important information on this unit.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on ethical considerations in marketing contexts.
Synthesise a range of perspectives on marketing strategies in practice to independently and collaboratively identify and effectively communicate potential solution/s.
Identify factors that influence the competitive position of a firm.
Reflect on team processes that enable industry analysis, assessment of marketing opportunities and the development of potential solution/s.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Professional practice: Reflections on ethics and teamwork

title: Digital Marketing
syllabus_overview: Business today is increasingly confronted with the need to participate in and manage a real-time digital environment. Marketers are expected to adopt digital mindsets and be fluent with digital business strategies. Such understanding and skills help them to take advantage of digital technologies to gain a competitive advantage. This unit develops students’ knowledge and skills in digital marketing. The unit focuses on the key concepts and frameworks used in digital marketing strategy, implementation and practice. Attention is given to the use of contemporary digital marketing applications in value creation, customer acquisition, customer retention and development.
learning_outcomes: Critically apply the theories and concepts underpinning digital marketing.
Critically analyse and evaluate the digital marketing strategies of a business
Design digital marketing strategies to launch and grow a digital business and communicate the strategies in a professional manner to the audience, individually and in collaboration

assessment_tasks.task_name: Skills development: Digital marketing in practice
Skills development: Competitive digital marketing analysis

title: Sales and Personal Selling
syllabus_overview: Sales is an important function in any commercial organisation. Within organisations, salespeople play a crucial role in aligning their organisation's offerings with customers’ needs, and in maximising value creation for both the customer and the selling firm.
